messages.body_plain:
Sorry for the frustration.

Can you get to a command window (type window + R, type "cmd", hit enter), then type "g++ -v"? Please report the result.

It should say "4.6.3" or "4.9". If it doesn't, you don't have the tool chain installed correctly.

I think Eric has a script to check installation on Windows. I don't have the location on hand.

Daniel

messages.subject: Joint modelling - continuous and Time-to-Event model
messages.subject_clean: Joint modelling - continuous and Time-to-Event model
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

i am quite new to STAN and was wondering what the possibility is in STAN to estimate a joint model of continuous and Time-to-Event data. Is STAN a good and robust platform for this kind of analysis (what about convergence and fitting?)? As well, if there is any example code or past experience to share as a starting point, i would be very happy to take.
Thanks very much.

Best,
Camille

messages.subject: Innocent little models won't fit in rstanarm
messages.subject_clean: Innocent little models won't fit in rstanarm
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I ran stan_glm() and it crashed 2 of the chains!  Data are attached.  My R code is below, then I'll show you the output in the R console.  There's no way this should be happening!
A

--

library("rstanarm")
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
library("arm")
library("loo")

wells <- read.csv("wells.csv")
N <- nrow(wells)
dist100 <- wells$dist100
arsenic <- wells$arsenic
y <- wells$y

bayes_fit_3 <- stan_glm(y ~ dist100 + arsenic, family=binomial(link="logit"), prior=normal(0, 10, autoscale=FALSE))
# This fits just fine.

log_arsenic <- log(arsenic)
bayes_fit_3a <- stan_glm(y ~ dist100 + log(arsenic), family=binomial(link="logit"), prior=normal(0, 10, autoscale=FALSE))
# This fits fine too.

bayes_fit_4a <- stan_glm(y ~ dist100 + log_arsenic + dist100:log_arsenic, family=binomial(link="logit"), prior=normal(0, 10, autoscale=FALSE))
# This one also works.

bayes_fit_4 <- stan_glm(y ~ dist100 + arsenic + dist100:arsenic, family=binomial(link="logit"), prior=normal(0, 10, autoscale=FALSE))
# This one has big, big problems  It runs really slowly and then returns these warnings:
Warning messages:
1: There were 981 divergent transitions after warmup. Increasing adapt_delta above 0.95 may help. See
http://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#divergent-transitions-after-warmup
2: There were 1 chains where the estimated Bayesian Fraction of Missing Information was low. See
http://mc-stan.org/misc/warnings.html#bfmi-low
3: Examine the pairs() plot to diagnose sampling problems
4: Markov chains did not converge! Do not analyze results!

# Why such problems?  The simple glm(y ~ dist100 + arsenic + dist100:arsenic, family=binomial(link="logit")) runs just fine, it's not like the variables are collinear or anything.  And in my stan_glm run I had proper priors.  Sure, N(0,10) is vague, but it's not _that_ vague.

# And now the model that fails:

noise <- array(rnorm(5*n), c(n, 5))
write.table(noise, "noise.txt")           # File is attached so this can be reproduced
bayes_fit_4b <- stan_glm(y ~ dist100 + log_arsenic + dist100:log_arsenic + noise, family=binomial(link="logit"), prior=normal(0, 10, autoscale=FALSE))
# See error messages below.

messages.subject: another rstanarm bug, this time with k-fold cross-validation, kfold()
messages.subject_clean: another rstanarm bug, this time with k-fold cross-validation, kfold()
messages.body_plain:
So.  I wanted to crate a model where loo would fail.  I did so using fake-data simulation, creating 5 random predictors that were correlated 0.8 with each other:

library("rstanarm")
options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores())
library("arm")
library("MASS")      # needed for mvrnorm()

n <- 200
k <- 5
rho <- 0.8
Sigma <- rho*array(1, c(k,k)) + (1-rho)*diag(k)
X <- mvrnorm(n, rep(0,k), Sigma)
b <- -2 + (1:k)
sigma <- 2
z <- rlogis(n, X %*% b, 1)
y <- ifelse(z>0, 1, 0)

## First I fit the full model:
fit_1 <- stan_glm(y ~ X, family=binomial(link="logit"), prior=normal(0, 10, autoscale=FALSE))
loo_1 <- loo(fit_1)
## I got this warning:

Warning message:
Found 23 observations with a pareto_k > 0.7. With this many problematic observations we recommend calling 'kfold' with argument 'K=10' to perform 10-fold cross-validation rather than LOO.

## OK, fine.  So I do 10-fold cross-validation:
kfold_1 <- kfold(fit_1, K=10)
print(kfold_1)
## And this works just fine.

## Now I want to compare to a model removing predictor 1
Z <- X[,2:5]
fit_2 <- stan_glm(y ~ Z, family=binomial(link="logit"), prior=normal(0, 10, autoscale=FALSE))
kfold_2 <- kfold(fit_2, K=10)
print(kfold_2)
## This works fine too.

## Then I try putting X[,2:5] right into the model (instead of giving it the new name Z):
fit_2 <- stan_glm(y ~ X[,2:5], family=binomial(link="logit"), prior=normal(0, 10, autoscale=FALSE))
## This works fine.
## But then I try the next step:
kfold_2 <- kfold(fit_2, K=10)
## And I get an error message:

Fitting model 1 out of 10
Error in X[, 2:5] : incorrect number of dimensions

## Whassup??  The model fit fine. So why the problem with kfold()?

A

messages.subject_clean: Joint modelling - continuous and Time-to-Event model
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Stan is great for this kind of stuff. There is just the usual pill to swallow when you do Bayesian TTE that you need either a parametric baseline hazard or some non-parametric variant. In short: Partial likelihood is not enough.

Other than that I can tell from my own experience that you need to watch out for the parametrization. Standard TTE distributions parametrization are not always optimal for sampling; at least in my problems I came across. However, you are new, so you should get started and do those parametrization games in a second step (pairs plots, etc.).

Sebastian

On Wednesday, February 1, 2017 at 12:54:25 AM UTC-5, Andrew Gelman wrote:
> There's no way this should be happening!

Way. If you have interaction terms and / or polynomials, then the derived variables have weird units and weird associations with the constituent variables, and adjusting the priors marginally is insufficient to achieve good performance from Stan. If you use the QR reparameterization like the documentation / vignettes / us suggest, then it is fine:

library(rstanarm)
data(wells)
wells$dist100 <- wells$dist / 100
whatever <- normal(0,10)
bayes_fit_4a <- stan_glm(switch ~ dist100 * log(arsenic), data = wells,
                         family=binomial(link="logit"), QR = TRUE, prior = whatever)

Ben

messages.body_plain: So... kfold attempts to account for the fact that sometimes data is specified using the data argument to stan_glm and other times using the global environment. When no data argument is specified it needs to construct a data frame that it can use to refit the model K times (each time modifying that data frame to drop the right set of observation). So it constructs a data frame consisting of the 2nd through 5th columns of X because that's what you implicitly told it was your data. But now when we need to go refit the model how is the formula including X[, 2:5] supposed to be interpreted relative to this data frame? There are ways around this but so far they seem to introduce other complications that are even more annoying.

messages.subject: Re: Innocent little models won't fit in rstanarm
messages.subject_clean: Innocent little models won't fit in rstanarm
messages.body_plain:
I actually think rstanarm is behaving properly here in the sense that this is not happening because of a bug in the code but rather because of model that's actually trickier than it seems. It's just that the model that gives divergence warnings and the one that fails entirely are challenging for Stan (for the reasons Ben mentioned). But I was able to successfully run the model (using the attached noise.txt) in three different ways:

(a) using Ben's QR trick: see his response above

(b) setting autoscale=TRUE (or omitting it) to let rstanarm do the rescaling of the prior (it really doesn't like normal(0,10) with autoscale=FALSE for this model):

bayes_fit_4b2 <- stan_glm(

  y ~ dist100 + log_arsenic + dist100:log_arsenic + noise,
  family=binomial(link="logit"),

  prior=normal(0, 10, autoscale=TRUE)
)

and (c) keeping autoscale=FALSE but reducing the range for random inits using init_r:

bayes_fit_4b2 <- stan_glm(

  y ~ dist100 + log_arsenic + dist100:log_arsenic + noise,
  family=binomial(link="logit"),

  prior=normal(0, 10, autoscale=FALSE),
  init_r = 0.1
)

The model fits without warning for me using methods (a), (b), and (c), although they're not all equally efficient.

Jonah

P.S. The wells dataset is actually included in rstanarm (because it's used in one of the vignettes) so you don't need to load it separately. See help("rstanarm-datasets") for the full list of included datasets. Also, this isn't part of the problem in this case, but I highly recommend using model formula + data when fitting the model instead of assigning things to the global environment and then just using the formula without data. The reason is partly related to the problem with kfold, but in general R is just so much more robust to errors if objects named in formulas are looked for inside other objects (e.g. data frames) rather than in environments.

On Wednesday, February 1, 2017 at 1:16:54 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> What does (b) rescaling the prior do to the model?
>
> - Bob

rstanarm let's you either specify prior scales directly or specify them in terms of the scales of the predictors. If auto-rescaling is enabled then rstanarm will adjust the specified prior scale(s) using information about the scale(s) of the predictor variable(s). For example

prior = normal(0, 10, autoscale=FALSE)

means that the prior actually used is normal(0, 10), but

prior = normal(0, 10, autoscale=TRUE)

means that the prior actually used is normal(0, 10 * scale_adjustment_factor), where the scale_adjustment factor is computed in the same way as it was in the original arm package. If you have the most recent version of rstanarm installed (via install.packages("rstanarm")) then the precise details about how that adjustment works are described in the doc for the "autoscale" argument at help("priors", package = "rstanarm").

Jonah

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: Innocent little models won't fit in rstanarm
messages.body_plain:
That really is a data-driven prior.  And it's turned on by
default.

For everyone else's benefit:

  autoscale
  A logical scalar, defaulting to TRUE. If TRUE then the scales of the priors
  on the intercept and regression coefficients may be additionally modified
  internally by rstanarm as follows. First, if the outcome is Gaussian, the
  prior scales for the intercept and coefficients are multiplied by 2*sd(y).
  Additionally, if the QR argument to the model fitting function (e.g. stan_glm)
  is FALSE then: for a predictor with only one value nothing is changed; for a
  predictor x with exactly two unique values, we take the user-specified (or
  default) scale(s) for the selected priors and divide by the range of x; for
  a predictor x with more than two unique values, we divide the prior
  scale(s) by 2*sd(x).

- Bob

> On Feb 1, 2017, at 1:33 PM, Jonah Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Wednesday, February 1, 2017 at 1:16:54 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> What does (b) rescaling the prior do to the model?
>
> - Bob
>
> rstanarm let's you either specify prior scales directly or specify them in terms of the scales of the predictors. If auto-rescaling is enabled then rstanarm will adjust the specified prior scale(s) using information about the scale(s) of the predictor variable(s). For example
>
> prior = normal(0, 10, autoscale=FALSE)
>
> means that the prior actually used is normal(0, 10), but
>
> prior = normal(0, 10, autoscale=TRUE)
>
> means that the prior actually used is normal(0, 10 * scale_adjustment_factor), where the scale_adjustment factor is computed in the same way as it was in the original arm package. If you have the most recent version of rstanarm installed (via install.packages("rstanarm")) then the precise details about how that adjustment works are described in the doc for the "autoscale" argument at help("priors", package = "rstanarm").
>
> Jonah
>

It used to be a lot less apparent but in the most recent release we've done a few things to make it more clear:

(1) We added the autoscale argument directly to the functions for specifying priors (instead of as a separate and easily overlooked argument 'scaled' to the modeling function, which was how arm did it)

(2) We introduced the prior_summary function which, for any rstanarm model, shows both the user-specified scales and the adjusted scales (if auto-scaling is on)

Regarding whether or not this is a good idea in general I have mixed feelings. On the one hand it's obviously not truly full Bayes anymore. On the other hand how else could we have default priors that aren't totally useless? This is one of the hard things about developing a package like rstanarm that attempts remove barriers to entry while still maintaining its integrity, so to speak. I think Andrew's original justification for it similar to what he says in this blog post:

http://andrewgelman.com/2016/03/25/28321/

Yup.  Andrew does what other people call "empirical Bayes" but
won't call it that.

I don't see how a hyperprior on the scale of predictors is going
to help here.

  vector[K] beta;
  real beta;
  real<lower=0> sigma;

  mu_beta ~ ...
  sigma_beta ~ ...
  beta ~ normal(mu_beta, sigma_beta);

  y ~ normal(x * beta, sigma_y);

(or maybe mu_beta is set to 0?) seems very different than

  beta ~ normal(0, SIGMA);
  y ~ normal(x ./ x_two_sigma * beta, sigma_y);

where SIGMA is some constant.

- Bob

Yeah, that was a large part of the motivation for adding the prior_summary function. For example, for a linear regression model the printed output from prior_summary looks like this:

> prior_summary(fit)

Priors for model 'fit'
------

Intercept (after predictors centered)
 ~ normal(location = 0, scale = 10)
     **adjusted scale = 120.54

Coefficients
 ~ normal(location = [0,0,0,...], scale = [10,10,10,...])
     **adjusted scale = [33.75, 0.49, 0.88,...]

Auxiliary (sigma)
 ~ cauchy(location = 0, scale = 5)

------
See help('prior_summary.stanreg') for more details

and the object actually returned by prior_summary also includes the stuff that get's shortened to "..." in the printed output. If the user follows the message at the bottom to check out the help page they'll see a short explanation and pointers to where they can find even more information if desired.

Oh, and take a look at the adjusted scale values. For the coefficients they range from 34 to less than 1 (for the intercept it's even > 100). That's why -- despite my own misgivings -- I've come around to the idea of having autoscale default to TRUE. How else can we avoid most models running into trouble if run with default settings?

messages.body_plain:
I found this paper quite informative. In particular, I had been playing around with a model that had drastically different n_eff if I use the centered parameteriation or the non-centered parameterization (centered was better, the original data set was about 120X500 with 120 groups having about 500 data points each). I suppose I had been working under the assumption that it was always better to use non-centered parameterization in cases like this, which is why it took me so long to try it the other way.

One part of the paper I wasn't entirely clear on was Figure 8. Am I correct that this was created by adjusting the value of alpha in the transformed data section of the "Generate One-Way Normal Pseudo-data" (and then running the respective other models and gathering the statistics)? If this is the case, then it looks like if you had standardized the data, then the centered parameterization is preferred. Also if this is the case, then it becomes obvious why the non-centered parameterization didn't work well in my case: the standard deviation of my data was closer to 0.08, well inside the region where centered parameterization produced more effective samples per unit time.

I would be curious how important other factors are in driving the outperformance of one versus the other. For instance, the number of groups vs. the amount of data or the standard deviation within the groups vs. the standard deviation of all the data.

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, February 1, 2017 at 3:49:08 PM UTC-5, John Hall wrote:
> For instance, the number of groups vs. the amount of data or the standard deviation within the groups vs. the standard deviation of all the data.

It's not so much the amount of data but rather how informative the data is about the parameters. You can have a small dataset that is informative enough to really pin down parameters and you can have large datasets where the data doesn't provide too much information about the parameters. If you want to see this in action in a simple example then you can play around with the eight schools example. If you leave the number of data points at 8 but modify y (or sigma) to make the data more or less informative about the parameters then which parameterization to use will depend on how you scale y (or sigma). In all cases the amount of data remains the same.

Jonah

Well, not "data=data" but maybe "data=wells" isn't so bad? Unlike the list you need to (or needed to) manually create for rstan, for rstanarm it would just be the name of the data frame where the variables in the formula can be found. I understand the appeal of not needing to do that, but I think that's outweighed by the mess it causes for software development. Here's a pros/cons list:

Cons of searching for data in global (or local) environment if not specified:

1) Takes developers a lot more time to add anything new to rstanarm because it's not easy to ensure that the data is handled appropriately. This is not an exaggeration: at most 1/4 of the time I spent implementing kfold was getting the algorithm right and the rest was spent on avoiding errors when people specify data without a data argument. And even after all that time there are apparently still cases when it doesn't work!)
2) Inevitably more bugs because the internal code needs to be much more complicated and is harder to test
3) Easier for the user to make mistakes (need to be very vigilant about what's already in the global environment)
4) I could probably come up with a bunch more!

Pros of searching for data in global (or local) environment if not specified:

1) A little bit less typing for the user

Am I missing any other advantages other than a bit less typing? I really don't want to sacrifice the quality of the software just to avoid typing something like data=wells, but if there are other advantages I'm missing then maybe those will tip the scale.

Jonah

messages.subject: problems with "data frames"
messages.subject_clean: problems with "data frames"
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Jonah.  We can talk about it on Friday.  Short answer is that when working with data and fitting models it's a real pain in the ass to keep working with a data frame.  I actually don't like the whole "data frame" thing as it can act as a straitjacket, it's a Stata way of thinking.

Here's an example.  I start with this model (for simplicity I'm assuming we have a stan_logit() alias):

stan_logit(y ~ dist + arsenic)
or
stan_logit(y ~ dist + arsenic, data="wells")

Ok, fine so far.  Now I decide I want to code as dist/100:
dist100 <- dist/100
stan_logit(y ~ dist100 + arsenic)

That worked fine.  Now the alternative:
dist100 <- dist/100 INSIDE "wells"
stan_logit(y ~ dist100 + arsenic, data="wells")

So here's my question:  can I do this:
dist100 <- dist/100 INSIDE "wells"
in a reasonable way?

Right now I have to first pull dist out of wells, then compute dist100, then put it back into wells, something like this:
dist <- wells$dist
dist100 <- dist/100
APPEND wells with dist100
(I don't remember how to do that last command but I know it can be done in one line.)

Anyway, that's the point.  In the midst of running regressions I play with data, for example creating a new predictor:
x_avg <- (x1 + x2 + x3)/3
or whatever.
If I have to keep putting things into the data frame just to run my regressions, that's a pain in the ass.  It's _not_ just "a bit more typing," it's actual additional lines of code, it makes things harder to follow.

In Stata world, you have a big data matrix and then pull out columns of it.  I don't see this as being R world.

A

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Article or proper explanation of the "Matt trick" / non-centered parameterization
messages.body_plain:
These concerns are best analyzed empirically using Stan’s diagnostics.
See, for example, https://github.com/betanalpha/knitr_case_studies/tree/master/divergences_and_bias.

> On Feb 1, 2017, at 4:15 PM, Jonah Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> On Wednesday, February 1, 2017 at 3:49:08 PM UTC-5, John Hall wrote:
> > For instance, the number of groups vs. the amount of data or the standard deviation within the groups vs. the standard deviation of all the data.
>
> It's not so much the amount of data but rather how informative the data is about the parameters. You can have a small dataset that is informative enough to really pin down parameters and you can have large datasets where the data doesn't provide too much information about the parameters. If you want to see this in action in a simple example then you can play around with the eight schools example. If you leave the number of data points at 8 but modify y (or sigma) to make the data more or less informative about the parameters then which parameterization to use will depend on how you scale y (or sigma). In all cases the amount of data remains the same.
>
> Jonah

Ok we'll talk more Friday about this but just a few quick things before then:

On Wed, Feb 1, 2017 at 5:23 PM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:

> Also I think that things that can be done in lm() and glm() should be doable in stan_lm() and stan_glm().

I don't fully trust that this always works properly in lm and glm either. I believe that the lm and glm functions fit the models correctly but I have no doubt that there are methods written for those fitted model objects somewhere with subtle bugs because of this issue.

> So here's my question:  can I do this:
> dist100 <- dist/100 INSIDE "wells"
> in a reasonable way?

Without having to load extra packages (e.g. Hadley's dplyr) you can use any of the following:

wells$dist100 <- wells$dist / 100

wells$dist100 <- with(wells, dist / 100)
wells <- within(wells, dist100 <- dist / 100)

Not super elegant, I admit, but there are options.

> If I have to keep putting things into the data frame just to run my regressions, that's a pain in the ass.  It's _not_ just "a bit more typing," it's actual additional lines of code, it makes things harder to follow.

Ok yeah that can definitely be a pain in the ass. There's probably some middle ground we can find when we discuss on Friday.

Jonah

P.S. I'm reminded of your blog post <http://andrewgelman.com/2015/12/23/r-sucks-2/> about how frustrating it was when you found there was a dataset "attitude" automatically loaded into your R session. That's similar to the feeling everyone who writes software packages has whenever we think about searching for variables in the global environment. You just never quite know what you're going to find!

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Article or proper explanation of the "Matt trick" / non-centered parameterization
messages.body_plain:
Diagnostics are good, but I'm also trying to develop some sort of intuition surrounding the issue. Thus, Jonah's advice to play around with sigma in the 8 schools problem was a good one.

For instance, if I multiply sigma by 100, then the non-centered has significantly more n_eff than centered. And the reverse if I divide by 100. This is similar to the figure from the paper in that the lower standard deviation favors the centered approach.

The degree of pooling seems to matter quite a bit. In this case, looking at something like the average sigma vs. the mean value of tau gave a better indication of whether the centered or the non-centered would be better than just looking at the average of the sigmas. But this probably only works because each group has one member. So probably more generally, I would refer to the Table 18.4 on page 394 of Gelman and Hill. The more pooling there is, the more reason to use the non-centered parameterization.

On a somewhat related topic, Stan's documentation could do a little better on page 325 with a heading of non-centered parameterization and the text that follows is:

When there is a lot of data, such a hierarchical model can be made much more efficient
by shifting the data’s correlation with the parameters to the hyperparameters. Similar
to the funnel example, this will be much more efficient in terms of effective sample
size when there is not much data (see (Betancourt and Girolami, 2013)).

which is not exactly the easiest to follow. And honestly I think there is a typo here. The paragraph before actually makes pretty clear to use the centered parameterization when there is a lot of data (which I wish I had read before). This starts out talking about "when there is a lot of data," which is the opposite of the use case of non-centered parameterization. I would re-write this as

messages.body_plain:
Hi, Jonah and Ben.  We can talk more at our meeting about this.  I don't have a clear sense of how best to recommend informative priors in practice, and this was coming up when I was writing my chapter.  So we'll have a lot to talk about!
A

> On Feb 1, 2017, at 12:18 PM, Jonah Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> I actually think rstanarm is behaving properly here in the sense that this is not happening because of a bug in the code but rather because of model that's actually trickier than it seems. It's just that the model that gives divergence warnings and the one that fails entirely are challenging for Stan (for the reasons Ben mentioned). But I was able to successfully run the model (using the attached noise.txt) in three different ways:
>
> (a) using Ben's QR trick: see his response above
>
> (b) setting autoscale=TRUE (or omitting it) to let rstanarm do the rescaling of the prior (it really doesn't like normal(0,10) with autoscale=FALSE for this model):
>
> bayes_fit_4b2 <- stan_glm(
>   y ~ dist100 + log_arsenic + dist100:log_arsenic + noise,
>   family=binomial(link="logit"),
>   prior=normal(0, 10, autoscale=TRUE)
> )
>
> and (c) keeping autoscale=FALSE but reducing the range for random inits using init_r:
>
> bayes_fit_4b2 <- stan_glm(
>   y ~ dist100 + log_arsenic + dist100:log_arsenic + noise,
>   family=binomial(link="logit"),
>   prior=normal(0, 10, autoscale=FALSE),
>   init_r = 0.1
> )
>
> The model fits without warning for me using methods (a), (b), and (c), although they're not all equally efficient.
>
> Jonah
>
> P.S. The wells dataset is actually included in rstanarm (because it's used in one of the vignettes) so you don't need to load it separately. See help("rstanarm-datasets") for the full list of included datasets. Also, this isn't part of the problem in this case, but I highly recommend using model formula + data when fitting the model instead of assigning things to the global environment and then just using the formula without data. The reason is partly related to the problem with kfold, but in general R is just so much more robust to errors if objects named in formulas are looked for inside other objects (e.g. data frames) rather than in environments.

messages.body_plain:
I really don't like this idea that I'm working "out of the global environment."  I'd like to do everything within the local environment.  That's what's standard in R, and I just want to do standard R.  For example, if you're working in a function in R, you use the local environment.

I feel like you (Bob) have the impression that I want to use global variables (and maybe GOTO statements).  But that's not it at all.  In R there's always a well-defined local environment (or, at least, I think there is), and that's what I think should be used.  NOT the global environment. I never wanted that.

A

> thing.  I hope Andrew's not writing the new book to lean heavily
> on that.
>
> - Bob
>
>> On Feb 1, 2017, at 11:44 AM, Jonah Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>>
>> So... kfold attempts to account for the fact that sometimes data is specified using the data argument to stan_glm and other times using the global environment. When no data argument is specified it needs to construct a data frame that it can use to refit the model K times (each time modifying that data frame to drop the right set of observation). So it constructs a data frame consisting of the 2nd through 5th columns of X because that's what you implicitly told it was your data. But now when we need to go refit the model how is the formula including X[, 2:5] supposed to be interpreted relative to this data frame? There are ways around this but so far they seem to introduce other complications that are even more annoying.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] In R, I want to use local, not global, environment
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] In R, I want to use local, not global, environment
messages.body_plain:
We've been (at least Ive been) a bit sloppy with terminology and I think that's leading to some misunderstanding. Some of it has to do with the global environment but some of it is still a problem with local environments too.

The real issue is that R will look for variables in parent environments (and then keep looking if it doesn't find them).  Often the global environment is the only one but it can also include local environments that themselves are parents to other environments and this is often just as problematic. It's really useful for some things but anything that isn't taken directly from user specified input can lead to trouble when it needs to be used later. Any specification of data that isn't directly input by the user is messy even if the data exists in an intermediate environment between the modeling function and the global environment. So even behavior that is natural to R is actually problematic for development of modeling software  because the same problem can occur no matter if the sole parent environment is the global environment or if there are layers of environments in between.

Ultimately it's really just that it's much harder to make robust software when you have to deal with R's handling of environments (not just global) instead of relying on the user to just tell you exactly what to use.

I definitely see why being stricter about this can be a pain from a user perspective, so hopefully we can find a good compromise.

Jonah

> Hi, Jonah and Ben.  We can talk more at our meeting about this.  I don't have a clear sense of how best to recommend informative priors in practice, and this was coming up when I was writing my chapter.  So we'll have a lot to talk about!

> > On Feb 1, 2017, at 12:18 PM, Jonah Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > I actually think rstanarm is behaving properly here in the sense that this is not happening because of a bug in the code but rather because of model that's actually trickier than it seems. It's just that the model that gives divergence warnings and the one that fails entirely are challenging for Stan (for the reasons Ben mentioned). But I was able to successfully run the model (using the attached noise.txt) in three different ways:
> >
> > (a) using Ben's QR trick: see his response above
> >
> > (b) setting autoscale=TRUE (or omitting it) to let rstanarm do the rescaling of the prior (it really doesn't like normal(0,10) with autoscale=FALSE for this model):
> >
> > bayes_fit_4b2 <- stan_glm(
> >   y ~ dist100 + log_arsenic + dist100:log_arsenic + noise,
> >   family=binomial(link="logit"),
> >   prior=normal(0, 10, autoscale=TRUE)
> > )
> >
> > and (c) keeping autoscale=FALSE but reducing the range for random inits using init_r:
> >
> > bayes_fit_4b2 <- stan_glm(
> >   y ~ dist100 + log_arsenic + dist100:log_arsenic + noise,
> >   family=binomial(link="logit"),
> >   prior=normal(0, 10, autoscale=FALSE),
> >   init_r = 0.1
> > )
> >
> > The model fits without warning for me using methods (a), (b), and (c), although they're not all equally efficient.
> >
> > Jonah
> >
> > P.S. The wells dataset is actually included in rstanarm (because it's used in one of the vignettes) so you don't need to load it separately. See help("rstanarm-datasets") for the full list of included datasets. Also, this isn't part of the problem in this case, but I highly recommend using model formula + data when fitting the model instead of assigning things to the global environment and then just using the formula without data. The reason is partly related to the problem with kfold, but in general R is just so much more robust to errors if objects named in formulas are looked for inside other objects (e.g. data frames) rather than in environments.

messages.subject: Regression: removing predictors increases sampling time
messages.subject_clean: Regression: removing predictors increases sampling time
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to solve a regression problem using a log-normal distribution whose location and scale both depend polynomially on the predictor, however when I reduce the degree of the scale's polynomial, the sampling time increases (even though the model gets simpler).

Here's a model that captures what I'm trying to do:

> data {
>     int<lower=1> C;                   // dimension (degree) location regressors.
>     int<lower=1> D;                   // dimension of scale regressors.
>     int<lower=1> N;                   // number of data points.
>     matrix[N, C] L;                     // location regressors.
>     matrix<lower=0>[N, D] S;    // scale regressors.
>     vector<lower=0>[N] Y;         // outcomes.
> }
> parameters {
>     vector[C] alpha;
>     vector<lower=0>[D] beta;
> }
> model {
>     Y ~ lognormal(L * alpha, S * beta);
>
>     alpha ~ normal(0, 1);
>     beta   ~ normal(0, 1);
> }

And here are the results of some timed runs on my data:

> C = 4, D = 2:
> 1 loop, best of 3: 32.9 s per loop
>
> C = 4, D = 3:
> 1 loop, best of 3: 24 s per loop
>
> C = 4, D = 4:
> 1 loop, best of 3: 12.6 s per loop

In this case N was 500 (but the issue showed up on my full dataset of about 9000 points); I initialised using fixed values; and all three inferences pretty much agree. I've applied this model to random data and the issue didn't really seem to show up, so I think it's data-specific.

I'm trying to figure out — and I'd be grateful if someone could provide an explanation — why the simpler model can take longer to sample. I've re-implemented the model in quite a few ways, but the issue remains. At this point I think it has to do with what Bob Carpenter mentioned in this answer <https://groups.google.com/d/msg/stan-users/9AkpbQxQ_f0/kAqhQ2HKBgAJ>, regarding the automatic differentiation that's happening behind the scenes, but I'd like some clarity so I know how to handle these situations in the future.

A few quick notes:
I wanted the model to be able to handle non-polynomial regression too, and allow for separate location and scale regressors.
Generally my values are binned, so there are quite a few duplicates — I've done some experiments and found that the sampler performs much faster if I use a ragged data structure rather than the flat one I've shown above. It might be worth mentioning this in the section on flat/ragged data structures (Chapter 15 in 2.14) in the manual? (Since in this case the vectorised implementation is in fact slower.)
In the end I'm probably going to set C = D and use all the regressors for both parameters anyway, because I'm not trying to do model comparison; however, this is bugging me.
Thanks,
Kevin

> On Tuesday, January 31, 2017 at 12:18:25 PM UTC-8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > Just to be clear, those are WARNINGS, not errors.
> >
> > The first one is indicating that given y is
> > a derived quantity, you may need a Jacobian adjustment for
> > it.  In this case, you don't, because you're just munging
> > data shape and there's no nonlinear transform. Stan can't
> > always figure that out.  Rather than this:
> >
> > > for (n in 1:N1)
> > >     y[n] = y1[n];
> > >   for (n in 1:N2)
> > >     y[N1 + n] = y2[n];
> > >
> > >   y ~ multi_normal(mu, Sigma);
> >
> > you can just do this:
> >
> >   y[1:N1] = y1;
> >   y[N1 + n:N1 + N2] = y2;
> >
> > I'm afraid we don't have append for arrays, but we should,
> > so I'm adding a feature request:
> >
> > https://github.com/stan-dev/math/issues/481
> >
> > The second issue is because there were numerical problems with the
> > run.  If you only get a handful of those, the problem can usually
> > be mitigated by increasing the adapt_delta control parameter.
> >
> > You might also want to add tighter/narrower tailed priors,
> > which can avoid parameters getting into extreme values.
> >
> > - Bob

messages.body_plain:
On Wednesday, February 1, 2017 at 7:57:27 PM UTC+1, Jonah Gabry wrote:
> Regarding whether or not this is a good idea in general I have mixed feelings. On the one hand it's obviously not truly full Bayes anymore. On the other hand how else could we have default priors that aren't totally useless?

You can call them weakly informative priors. The scaling is based on the data, but since priors are wide, the amount of information used is weak and mainly takes into account the order of magnitude of the values. For example, if the measurements were heights of people, you could set non-data-dependent prior if you know whether the measurements are in mm, cm, inch, feet or m, but now you save some time by checking the order of magnitude from the data. You could make the default priors even wider if you want to make the even more weakly informative and of course autoscaling can give undesired results in case of outliers etc.

Aki

The problem is firstly that most users, especially of rstanarm, do not
even consider thinking about the priors like this (which is one of the
reasons I’m hesitant about pushing packages like these).  Even if
they were interested, however, we have a lot of work to go in
improving pedagogy that supports how to do this correctly.

Either we autoscale so that users don’t have to think and we get a
larger userbase (hopefully to be funneled into Stan proper, although
that’ll be a slow trickle at best) or we force more principled inputs
about scales and watch as the user base plummets.

Good inferential practices are like vegetables for users.  They need
them but they really can’t be convinced of them and often the only
way we can get them to buy in is by covering them with a whole
bunch of sauce.

messages.subject: performance question / managing the AD stack
messages.subject_clean: performance question / managing the AD stack
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Managing the AD stack size is always critical in Stan applications as I am aware, but is it about sheer size or about values ever calculated?

So what I am doing is to calculate concentrations at different time-points in a multi-compartement system which are subject to dosing.

Say I have D = 10 dosing events and T = 100 time-points in a system with C=3 compartements. The data at hand is always observing only a single c_obs compartment out of the three. At the moment my Stan program will calculate a T * C matrix, then subset to the column c_obs of the matrix which I have observed. Therefore, I only need T variables out of the T*C.

My question now - is this inefficient? As alternative I could move C states from the first to the last time-point and along the way output the T states of the observed compartement.

So is it very costly to have many temporary AD variables around or should I try to avoid these?

Thanks much.

Sebastian

messages.body_plain:
While you're at it, you might consider adding a reference to Gelman and Hill chapter 21 as well. It has a formula 21.14 (and some R code below it) for calculating a lambda parameter that can be used to determine the amount of pooling at any level. It would be a useful diagnostic for whether one should use the non-centered parameterization in a hierarchical model (and in general would probably be a useful summary statistic to look at anyway).

On Wed, Feb 1, 2017 at 7:11 PM, Jonah Sol Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:

> You're right about that paragraph in the manual. Thanks for catching that. I can add this to the GitHub issue for edits to the manual for the next release.
>
> Jonah

> On Wed, Feb 1, 2017 at 6:43 PM John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > Diagnostics are good, but I'm also trying to develop some sort of intuition surrounding the issue. Thus, Jonah's advice to play around with sigma in the 8 schools problem was a good one.
> >
> > For instance, if I multiply sigma by 100, then the non-centered has significantly more n_eff than centered. And the reverse if I divide by 100. This is similar to the figure from the paper in that the lower standard deviation favors the centered approach.
> >
> > The degree of pooling seems to matter quite a bit. In this case, looking at something like the average sigma vs. the mean value of tau gave a better indication of whether the centered or the non-centered would be better than just looking at the average of the sigmas. But this probably only works because each group has one member. So probably more generally, I would refer to the Table 18.4 on page 394 of Gelman and Hill. The more pooling there is, the more reason to use the non-centered parameterization.
> >
> >
> > On a somewhat related topic, Stan's documentation could do a little better on page 325 with a heading of non-centered parameterization and the text that follows is:
> >
> > When there is a lot of data, such a hierarchical model can be made much more efficient
> > by shifting the data’s correlation with the parameters to the hyperparameters. Similar
> > to the funnel example, this will be much more efficient in terms of effective sample
> > size when there is not much data (see (Betancourt and Girolami, 2013)).
> >
> > which is not exactly the easiest to follow. And honestly I think there is a typo here. The paragraph before actually makes pretty clear to use the centered parameterization when there is a lot of data (which I wish I had read before). This starts out talking about "when there is a lot of data," which is the opposite of the use case of non-centered parameterization. I would re-write this as
> >
> > When there is not much data, a non-centered parameterization can be much more efficient in terms of effective sample size by shifting the data’s correlation with the parameters to the hyperparameters. (see (Betancourt and Girolami, 2013)).

> > On Wed, Feb 1, 2017 at 5:51 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > These concerns are best analyzed empirically using Stan’s diagnostics.
> > > See, for example, https://github.com/betanalpha/knitr_case_studies/tree/master/divergences_and_bias.

> > > > On Feb 1, 2017, at 4:15 PM, Jonah Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > >

> > > > On Wednesday, February 1, 2017 at 3:49:08 PM UTC-5, John Hall wrote:
> > > > > For instance, the number of groups vs. the amount of data or the standard deviation within the groups vs. the standard deviation of all the data.
> > > >
> > > > It's not so much the amount of data but rather how informative the data is about the parameters. You can have a small dataset that is informative enough to really pin down parameters and you can have large datasets where the data doesn't provide too much information about the parameters. If you want to see this in action in a simple example then you can play around with the eight schools example. If you leave the number of data points at 8 but modify y (or sigma) to make the data more or less informative about the parameters then which parameterization to use will depend on how you scale y (or sigma). In all cases the amount of data remains the same.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] performance question / managing the AD stack
messages.body_plain:
Operations add about 40 bytes to the stack.  And
each one adds a run-time virtual funcition call and
sometimes non-memory-local pointer chasing.

Our matrix operations try to be conservative with
memory, so there will be a breakeven point where doing
it by hand will be faster.

The arXiv paper goes into more detail.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Regression: removing predictors increases sampling time
messages.body_plain:
Model (mis)specification affects time.  So if the lower-order
thing doesn't fit as well (for example, there may be a lot of uncertainty),
it can slow things down.  You might want to check the scales of
your priors.

The log density and gradient will be faster for the simpler model,
but it may take leapfrog steps will be faster, but it may take more leapfrog
steps per iteration.

And don't forget it's all probabilistic, so you have to look
at multiple runs to get a trend.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Article or proper explanation of the "Matt trick" / non-centered parameterization
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Article or proper explanation of the "Matt trick" / non-centered parameterization
messages.body_plain:
This is a function I wrote to implement Gelman and HIll formula 21.14 with rstan. The higher lambda is the more benefit pooling there is and the greater the benefit from non-centered parameterization in hierarchical models.

lambda <- function(fit, ...) {
    extracted_fit <- rstan::extract(fit, permuted = TRUE, ...)
    N <- length(extracted_fit)
    result <- rep(NA, N)
    names(result) <- names(extracted_fit)
    for (i in 1:N) {
        extracted_fit_i <- extracted_fit[[i]]
        if (length(dim(extracted_fit_i)) == 1) next #only calculate if more than
                                                    #1 dimension
        e <- extracted_fit_i - mean(extracted_fit_i)
        result[i] <- 1 - var(apply(e, 2, mean)) / mean(apply(e, 1, var))
    }
    return(result)
}

messages.subject: Additive or multiplicative error terms
messages.subject_clean: Additive or multiplicative error terms
messages.body_plain:
This may be a very basic question, but here it is, anyway:
When dealing with strictly positive variables, people often use multiplicative error terms (with mean = 1 for the same reason that mean = 0 in additive error terms).
But there are at least two ways to write that in our model: using (for example) a lognormal distribution for Y / expected_Y, or using a normal distribution (centered at zero) for log (Y) - log (expected_Y). Yes they are mathematically equivalent, but is there any computational argument in favor of one over the other when it comes to Stan models?
Thanks!

How would you suggest to encode this ultimately ?

On Tuesday, July 5, 2016 at 9:06:58 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> That's what I kept asking you!  I use the Pareto(1.5) I borrowed
> from chapter 5 of BDA based on some logic Andrew no longer believes
> (it's derived as the Jacobian of a log uniform or something like that).
>
> I'm thinking it'd be nice to have versions of Beta and of
> the Dirichlet and of the Beta-binomial that work on the mean/precision
> scale (or maybe 1/precision or something like that).
>
> Yes, marginalizing a parameter out should be better in almost all
> cases (the exception would be if the geometry got ugly somehow
> from the marginalization but was well behaved without it).
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Jul 5, 2016, at 10:44 AM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> >
> > Hi, we're trying to fit a beta-binomial model as an overdispersed version of the binomial:
> > y_i ~ beta-binomial(n_i, alpha, beta);
> > But (alpha, beta) isn't the best parameterization.  We could do this:
> > alpha = mu*phi;
> > beta = (1-mu)*phi;
> > This takes us most of the way there:
> > mu is the mean, the probability parameter which we could then model on the logit scale, for example,
> > mu_i = invlogit(X_i*beta);
> > We could even program a beta_binomial_logit model.
> > But what about phi?  phi is restricted to be positive.  We can understand phi using the mean and variance of the distribution:
> > E(y) = n*alpha/(alpha+beta) = n*mu
> > var(y) = n*alpha*beta*(alpha+beta+n)/((alpha+beta)^2 * (alpha+beta+1)) = n*mu*(1-mu)*(phi+n)/(phi+1).
> > I'm assuming I didn't botch the algebra here.
> > If I got it right, the overdispersion factor is (phi+n)/(phi+1) which is kinda annoying in that the overdisp depends on n, but I guess that's the way things go.  Indeed, that makes sense:  if n=1 it's the Bernoulli model and there's no possibility of overdispersion.
> > Anyway, here's the question:  if we use this (or some other) parameterization, what's a good prior, what's a good way to model everything?  Does it makes sense to put a prior or a model on phi, or 1/phi, or log(phi)?  An exponential prior on phi?  Some other thing?
> > Another option would be to put overdispersion into the model using a component of variance:

messages.body_plain:
Cool, thanks. Your suggestions are now officially on the record:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/2122

(Scroll down to the bottom)

On Thu, Feb 2, 2017 at 1:29 PM John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:

> This is a function I wrote to implement Gelman and HIll formula 21.14 with rstan. The higher lambda is the more benefit pooling there is and the greater the benefit from non-centered parameterization in hierarchical models.
>
> lambda <- function(fit, ...) {
>     extracted_fit <- rstan::extract(fit, permuted = TRUE, ...)
>     N <- length(extracted_fit)
>     result <- rep(NA, N)
>     names(result) <- names(extracted_fit)
>     for (i in 1:N) {
>         extracted_fit_i <- extracted_fit[[i]]
>         if (length(dim(extracted_fit_i)) == 1) next #only calculate if more than
>                                                     #1 dimension
>         e <- extracted_fit_i - mean(extracted_fit_i)
>         result[i] <- 1 - var(apply(e, 2, mean)) / mean(apply(e, 1, var))
>     }
>     return(result)
> }

> On Thu, Feb 2, 2017 at 11:18 AM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > While you're at it, you might consider adding a reference to Gelman and Hill chapter 21 as well. It has a formula 21.14 (and some R code below it) for calculating a lambda parameter that can be used to determine the amount of pooling at any level. It would be a useful diagnostic for whether one should use the non-centered parameterization in a hierarchical model (and in general would probably be a useful summary statistic to look at anyway).

> > On Wed, Feb 1, 2017 at 7:11 PM, Jonah Sol Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > You're right about that paragraph in the manual. Thanks for catching that. I can add this to the GitHub issue for edits to the manual for the next release.
> > >
> > > Jonah

> > > On Wed, Feb 1, 2017 at 6:43 PM John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > > Diagnostics are good, but I'm also trying to develop some sort of intuition surrounding the issue. Thus, Jonah's advice to play around with sigma in the 8 schools problem was a good one.
> > > >
> > > > For instance, if I multiply sigma by 100, then the non-centered has significantly more n_eff than centered. And the reverse if I divide by 100. This is similar to the figure from the paper in that the lower standard deviation favors the centered approach.
> > > >
> > > > The degree of pooling seems to matter quite a bit. In this case, looking at something like the average sigma vs. the mean value of tau gave a better indication of whether the centered or the non-centered would be better than just looking at the average of the sigmas. But this probably only works because each group has one member. So probably more generally, I would refer to the Table 18.4 on page 394 of Gelman and Hill. The more pooling there is, the more reason to use the non-centered parameterization.
> > > >
> > > >
> > > > On a somewhat related topic, Stan's documentation could do a little better on page 325 with a heading of non-centered parameterization and the text that follows is:
> > > >
> > > > When there is a lot of data, such a hierarchical model can be made much more efficient
> > > > by shifting the data’s correlation with the parameters to the hyperparameters. Similar
> > > > to the funnel example, this will be much more efficient in terms of effective sample
> > > > size when there is not much data (see (Betancourt and Girolami, 2013)).
> > > >
> > > > which is not exactly the easiest to follow. And honestly I think there is a typo here. The paragraph before actually makes pretty clear to use the centered parameterization when there is a lot of data (which I wish I had read before). This starts out talking about "when there is a lot of data," which is the opposite of the use case of non-centered parameterization. I would re-write this as
> > > >
> > > > When there is not much data, a non-centered parameterization can be much more efficient in terms of effective sample size by shifting the data’s correlation with the parameters to the hyperparameters. (see (Betancourt and Girolami, 2013)).

> > > > On Wed, Feb 1, 2017 at 5:51 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:

> > > > > These concerns are best analyzed empirically using Stan’s diagnostics.
> > > > > See, for example, https://github.com/betanalpha/knitr_case_studies/tree/master/divergences_and_bias.

> > > > > > On Feb 1, 2017, at 4:15 PM, Jonah Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > >

> > > > > > On Wednesday, February 1, 2017 at 3:49:08 PM UTC-5, John Hall wrote:
> > > > > > > For instance, the number of groups vs. the amount of data or the standard deviation within the groups vs. the standard deviation of all the data.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > It's not so much the amount of data but rather how informative the data is about the parameters. You can have a small dataset that is informative enough to really pin down parameters and you can have large datasets where the data doesn't provide too much information about the parameters. If you want to see this in action in a simple example then you can play around with the eight schools example. If you leave the number of data points at 8 but modify y (or sigma) to make the data more or less informative about the parameters then which parameterization to use will depend on how you scale y (or sigma). In all cases the amount of data remains the same.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan team,

Would there be an avenue to pursuing a Google Summer of Code project related to Stan? I don't think you guys are on the list of mentoring organizations, but I would love to do something over the summer for the Stan project that would both be very educational for me and also very helpful to my own research. I'm starting to work with non-linear ODE systems now and need something like r's rootsolve package in Stan to avoid model spin-up to equilibrium.

The organization applications for GSoC are due on February 9th, so it might be too late already, but I just wanted to check in to see if Stan had any plans with Summer of Code. It could be a means of tackling some things on this page (https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Complex-ODE-Based-Models) through various projects that otherwise are outside the focus of primary development.

messages.body_plain:
Just to clarify if someone is counting votes for autoscaling: I don't like autoscaling priors although I can accept them as weakly informative priors if they are wide enough. I would prefer explicit scaling, so that modeler has to take the responsibility and thus think whether specific scaling is sensible. And naturally explicit scaling such as normalization or whitening is also using data and thus can be considered weakly informative scaling. I like to normalize covariates as then it's also easier to compare covariate effects (unless using APC or other predictive relevance estimates).

Aki

messages.subject: Saving samples of quantities computed based on variables defined in the model block
messages.subject_clean: Saving samples of quantities computed based on variables defined in the model block
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am currently implementing the generalized extreme value distribution in brms, which proved to be rather complicated.
Basically, I have to constrain the shape parameter xi to a certain interval based on other (predicted) model parameters to avoid
leaving the definition space of the response variable, which may cause many divergent transitions (the .stan file is attached).

These other predicted parameters are defined and computed in the model block, and not in transformed parameters,
to avoid that rstan is writing them to a csv-file in the temp folder even if not returned to the user later on
(at least this was rstan's behavior a few months ago when I moved most stuff to the model block).
These csv-files will get really big for huge models, which reportedly caused problems.

Long story short, I want to save the samples of the shape parameter xi, even though it depends on variables
defined in the model block. Or, I want to find a way to make sure that samples of quantities, which are never returned
to the user anyway, are not written to csv-files in the temp folder when defined in transformed parameters.

Many thanks for your help!

Best,
Paul

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Additive or multiplicative error terms
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Additive or multiplicative error terms
messages.body_plain:
They're not quite the same.  You get the Jacobian
adjustment in the lognormal, which will matter if
your Y is a parameter.  See the x in the denominator of
the pdf defined here:

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution

If Y is a constant, then that term gets dropped out if
you're using the sampling notation but not if you call
lognormal_lpdf(...) [as you would in a mixture model].

For efficiency, they're not much different.  There's
the extra log calculation, which you'd only want to do
once.  Then it's very similar up to the Jacobian adjustment.

There's also the transform if you have a positive constrained
location parameter mu (your expected_Y) or if you have
Y as parameter (as opposed to log Y).   In these cases, it
can be a bit more efficient to work on the unconstrained (log)
scale and then exp() up to the constrained positive scale
after the fact.

But I wouldn't worry about the efficiency difference for
these.

- Bob

> On Feb 2, 2017, at 2:54 PM, Vítor Margato <vitorma...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> This may be a very basic question, but here it is, anyway:
> When dealing with strictly positive variables, people often use multiplicative error terms (with mean = 1 for the same reason that mean = 0 in additive error terms).
> But there are at least two ways to write that in our model: using (for example) a lognormal distribution for Y / expected_Y, or using a normal distribution (centered at zero) for log (Y) - log (expected_Y). Yes they are mathematically equivalent, but is there any computational argument in favor of one over the other when it comes to Stan models?

> Here's an example.  I start with this model (for simplicity I'm assuming we have a stan_logit() alias):

> Ok, fine so far.  Now I decide I want to code as dist/100:

This is where I think it's super helpful for those *reading*
your work (which includes you in the future) to keep
everything together.  At this point, you have defined y somewere
before the last fit and define a new dist100 here and everything's
just sitting in the global environment ready to be modified.

Right.  You define

Which is playing with data.  And now the definition of the data
you're passing into the regression is spread through your history.

What Michael was arguing for is keeping the definition

Part II is just the technical issue.

But it's more confusing than I thought.  The core concept here is
that R passes by value and that the value of (y ~ x) is a formula.
But it looks like it behaves differently than ("y ~ x") in a function
context.

So this all looks OK:

```
> foo <- function(n) { x <- rnorm(n); y <- 100 * x + 200 + rnorm(n); return(lm(y ~ x)); }
> foo(10)

Call:
lm(formula = y ~ x)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)            x
      199.6        100.4
```

But now what happens when I quote that?

```
> bar <- function(n) { x <- rnorm(n); y <- 100 * x + 200 + rnorm(n); return(lm("y ~ x")); }
> bar(10)
Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'y' not found
```

Hmm.  I honestly don't know what's going on there.  But a little
spelunking shows me it's looking further up the environment chain:

```
> bar <- function(n) { x <- rnorm(n); y <- 100 * x + 200 + rnorm(n); return(lm("y ~ x")); }
> x <- rnorm(10); y <- rnorm(10)
> bar(10)

Call:
lm(formula = "y ~ x")

Coefficients:
(Intercept)            x
    0.02121     -0.20474
```

If you're in the top-level environment, now that x and y are defined,
quotes and no quotes appear to work the same way:

```
> lm(y ~ x)

Call:
lm(formula = y ~ x)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)            x
    0.02121     -0.20474

> lm("y ~ x")

Call:
lm(formula = "y ~ x")

Coefficients:
(Intercept)            x
    0.02121     -0.20474
```

I'm confused.  And rather frightened by this behavior.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Additive or multiplicative error terms
messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob! First of all, thanks for being so helpful.
I think I understand your reply, and I think I understand what you write here ("Jacobian Adjustments"): http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/mle-params.html
That said, I'm afraid I could have been more explicit about the two options I'm considering.
My dependent variable y is strictly positive, and I want to model it using an independent variable x (which, by the way, is non-negative) and a functional form f with parameters (say) a1 and a2.
I also have a vector of weights, since each x-y occurs in a number of observations (assumed to be iid). So I had two options in mind (see below), and wanted to know (a) whether they are truly equivalent and (b) whether one is much more efficient than the other. I'm guessing your response to (b) is no, but now I'm not sure about (a) anymore...
Thanks!

...
transformed parameters {
    real mean_log_y;
    for (i in 1: number_rows) {
        mean_log_y [i] = f (x [i], a1, a2); // This is not actual Stan code, of course
    }
}
model {
    a1 ~ ...;
    a2 ~ ...;
    sigma ~ ...; // Some strictly positive distribution
    for (i in 1: number_rows) {
        target += weight [i] * normal_lpdf (log_y [i] | mean_log_y [i], sigma);
    }
}

...
transformed parameters {
    real mean_log_y;
    for (i in 1: number_rows) {
        mean_log_y [i] = f (x [i], a1, a2); // This is not actual Stan code, of course
    }
}
model {
    a1 ~ ...;
    a2 ~ ...;
    sigma ~ ...; // Some strictly positive distribution
    for (i in 1: number_rows) {
        target += weight [i] * lognormal_lpdf (y [i] | mean_log_y [i] - sigma * sigma / 2, sigma); // I write it like this just so that the distribution has mean exp (mean_log_y)
    }
}

Em sexta-feira, 3 de fevereiro de 2017 05:16:06 UTC-2, Bob Carpenter escreveu:
> They're not quite the same.  You get the Jacobian
> adjustment in the lognormal, which will matter if
> your Y is a parameter.  See the x in the denominator of
> the pdf defined here:
>
> https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Log-normal_distribution
>
> If Y is a constant, then that term gets dropped out if
> you're using the sampling notation but not if you call
> lognormal_lpdf(...) [as you would in a mixture model].
>
> For efficiency, they're not much different.  There's
> the extra log calculation, which you'd only want to do
> once.  Then it's very similar up to the Jacobian adjustment.
>
> There's also the transform if you have a positive constrained
> location parameter mu (your expected_Y) or if you have
> Y as parameter (as opposed to log Y).   In these cases, it
> can be a bit more efficient to work on the unconstrained (log)
> scale and then exp() up to the constrained positive scale
> after the fact.
>
> But I wouldn't worry about the efficiency difference for
> these.
>
> - Bob
>
>
>
>
> > On Feb 2, 2017, at 2:54 PM, Vítor Margato <vitorma...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > This may be a very basic question, but here it is, anyway:
> > When dealing with strictly positive variables, people often use multiplicative error terms (with mean = 1 for the same reason that mean = 0 in additive error terms).
> > But there are at least two ways to write that in our model: using (for example) a lognormal distribution for Y / expected_Y, or using a normal distribution (centered at zero) for log (Y) - log (expected_Y). Yes they are mathematically equivalent, but is there any computational argument in favor of one over the other when it comes to Stan models?

messages.body_plain:
Ben,

Thanks for the speedy response. In order, and for others:

1. There appears to be no way to upload/scp/etc. a file to a shinyapps.io <http://shinyapps.io> server: it must all be bundled into the initial deploy.
2. Putting the .rds file on S3 then downloading this file after the application starts was successful in and of itself, but the `stan` called ignored it and tries to recompile.
3. I've been at the "build an R package" for several hours now. I create the package as such:

library(rstantools)
rstan_package_skeleton(name = "my_package", stan_files = "model.stan", path = "~/Documents/r-packages/")

The results of `R CMD check my_package` are as follows:

** testing if installed package can be loaded
Error in .doLoadActions(where, attach) :
  error in load action .__A__.1 for package RescueTimeEstimation: is(module, "character"): object 'm' not found

I tried following the relevant thread <https://groups.google.com/forum/#!msg/stan-users/JlYv7Rt6-zM/uq9y_ZjHAAAJ> in this group, which lead me to adding `useDynLib(RescueTimeEstimation, .registration = TRUE)` to the NAMESPACE file. From there, everything works. However (and crucially?), roxygen refuses to overwrite this file, so my NAMESPACE is left as is, instead of having all of the nice import statements I'm assuming I ultimately need.

4. Finally, while I have you: how do I actually use the model within the package? For example, how should the `stan(file = ...)` call look? I'm guessing it's not `stan(file = ../exec/model.stan)`. I assume this is an easy one; I'm not so experienced with C++ myself.

On Friday, February 3, 2017 at 1:44:28 AM UTC, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Thursday, February 2, 2017 at 5:07:08 PM UTC-5, William Wolf wrote:
> > When I deploy this app to shinyapps.io <http://shinyapps.io>, the model tries to recompile (resulting in a g++ error - presumably from lack of sufficient memory). Irrespective, I don't want this model to recompile in the first place: I'd like it to use the model.rds object I'd already built. Yes, I do include this object in the files uploaded to the shinyapps.io <http://shinyapps.io> server.
>
> I have never tried this before. It might be the case that if you upload the .stan file first and the .rds file second, it will get past the timestamp check that triggers a recompile. Otherwise, maybe it is possible to use clang++ instead of g++ on shinyapps.io <http://shinyapps.io>. The best answer is that if you want predictable behavior with precompiled models, you should just make a R package that contains them. See the rstan_package.skeleton function in the rstantools package or one of several packages like rstanarm that does it this way.
>
> Ben
>

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, and how would you recommend to handle the priors ?
I see  direct advice against using uniform but when I live priors out I get exceptions every now and then ...
  -Leon

On Fri, Feb 3, 2017 at 1:19 AM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> No, we never built that parameterization into Stan.
> It would still be a good idea to do that and a few
> other alternative parameterizations.
>
> You can still just encode it directly now.
>
> parameters {
>   real<lower = 0> kappa;     // prior count (plus K)
>   simplex[K] theta;          // prior mean
>
>
> model {
>
>   for (n in 1:N)
>     phi[n] ~ dirichlet(kappa * theta);
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Feb 2, 2017, at 3:24 PM, Leon Peshkin <pes...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > May I ask what is the bottom line on this one ?
> > Have you implemented (or close to ) this parametrization ?
> > How would you suggest to encode this ultimately ?
> >
> >    -Leon
> >
> > On Tuesday, July 5, 2016 at 9:06:58 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > That's what I kept asking you!  I use the Pareto(1.5) I borrowed
> > from chapter 5 of BDA based on some logic Andrew no longer believes
> > (it's derived as the Jacobian of a log uniform or something like that).
> >
> > I'm thinking it'd be nice to have versions of Beta and of
> > the Dirichlet and of the Beta-binomial that work on the mean/precision
> > scale (or maybe 1/precision or something like that).
> >
> > Yes, marginalizing a parameter out should be better in almost all
> > cases (the exception would be if the geometry got ugly somehow
> > from the marginalization but was well behaved without it).
> >
> > - Bob
> >
> >
> > > On Jul 5, 2016, at 10:44 AM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> > >
> > > Hi, we're trying to fit a beta-binomial model as an overdispersed version of the binomial:
> > > y_i ~ beta-binomial(n_i, alpha, beta);
> > > But (alpha, beta) isn't the best parameterization.  We could do this:
> > > alpha = mu*phi;
> > > beta = (1-mu)*phi;
> > > This takes us most of the way there:
> > > mu is the mean, the probability parameter which we could then model on the logit scale, for example,
> > > mu_i = invlogit(X_i*beta);
> > > We could even program a beta_binomial_logit model.
> > > But what about phi?  phi is restricted to be positive.  We can understand phi using the mean and variance of the distribution:
> > > E(y) = n*alpha/(alpha+beta) = n*mu
> > > var(y) = n*alpha*beta*(alpha+beta+n)/((alpha+beta)^2 * (alpha+beta+1)) = n*mu*(1-mu)*(phi+n)/(phi+1).
> > > I'm assuming I didn't botch the algebra here.
> > > If I got it right, the overdispersion factor is (phi+n)/(phi+1) which is kinda annoying in that the overdisp depends on n, but I guess that's the way things go.  Indeed, that makes sense:  if n=1 it's the Bernoulli model and there's no possibility of overdispersion.
> > > Anyway, here's the question:  if we use this (or some other) parameterization, what's a good prior, what's a good way to model everything?  Does it makes sense to put a prior or a model on phi, or 1/phi, or log(phi)?  An exponential prior on phi?  Some other thing?
> > > Another option would be to put overdispersion into the model using a component of variance:
> > > y_i ~ binomial(n_i, p_i);
> > > p_i = invlogit(X_i*beta + eta_i);
> > > eta_i ~ normal(0, sigma_eta);
> > > That should do the trick, but at a cost of adding a new parameter for each data point, which we should avoid, no?  Hence the motivation for the beta-binomial.
> > >
> > > What do people think?
> > > A

On Friday, February 3, 2017 at 2:48:25 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> We're not talking about a data frame here, but
> a list, right?  Don't data frames have to be square?

For rstan a list, for rstanarm preferably a data frame (although list can be made to work too, as data frames are just fancy lists). Data frames do not have to be square (if by square you mean same number of rows and columns).

>
> I have no idea what Stata does.

Somehow Stata is still in business despite only allowing one dataset in memory at a time!

>
> > Here's an example.  I start with this model (for simplicity I'm assuming we have a stan_logit() alias):
> >
> > stan_logit(y ~ dist + arsenic)
> > or
> > stan_logit(y ~ dist + arsenic, data="wells")
>
> Are you passing the name of a list or something here?

I think that's just a typo. "wells" wouldn't work here. It should just be the object wells, which is a data frame.

>
> > Ok, fine so far.  Now I decide I want to code as dist/100:
> > dist100 <- dist/100
> > stan_logit(y ~ dist100 + arsenic)
>
> This is where I think it's super helpful for those *reading*
> your work (which includes you in the future) to keep
> everything together.  At this point, you have defined y somewere
> before the last fit and define a new dist100 here and everything's
> just sitting in the global environment ready to be modified.

I completely agree, but I guess you were addressing to Andrew not me!

Jonah

On Friday, February 3, 2017 at 2:54:41 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> I'm confused.  And rather frightened by this behavior.
>
> - Bob

Indeed, it's very confusing! Imagine trying to write the internals for rstanarm or lme4 or any modeling package when users are allowed to specify unquoted formulas or quoted formulas and either with or without explicitly passing data. Of the time I spend on rstanarm, probably 75% is related to problems stemming from this behavior and it's really frustrating. We could have a package that is both more stable and has a lot more features if we put more restrictions than R typically does on how the user can specify models.

Jonah

messages.body_plain:
Suppose you have a 2-vector v and the function y = min(v).
Then the derivatives dy/dv[1] and dy/dv[2] are discontinuous
at the point where v[1] = v[2].  So you have to cross a discontinuity
in derivatives to move from (0.99, 1) to (1.01, 1).   That can
be problematic.  It's not that HMC will do the wrong thing, just
that it'll revert to a rejection sampler if it can't smoothly
cross boundaries;  how bad that is will vary from problem to problem.

- Bob

> On Feb 3, 2017, at 3:39 AM, Paul Buerkner <paul.b...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I am not sure that this is a problem. With min max I am just finding the range of values that are allowed for xi, so that the definition space of y is valid for all data thus getting rid of many divergent transitions..

>
> Am Freitag, 3. Februar 2017 07:16:12 UTC+1 schrieb Bob Carpenter:
>
> > On Feb 2, 2017, at 11:59 PM, andre.pfeuffer via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> >
> > Paul,
> >
> > I would fit towards the mean not towards the parameters of your distribution. Since the mean for GEV is not defined for zeta >= 1(shape)
> > maybe go for the mode instead. This doesn't change things for correctness point of view, but from sampling.
> >
> > The inv_logit with max/min, doesn't feel good to me in MCMC. Did you try to constrain your parameters? So they get truncated.
>
> Presumably the bad feeling is from the discontinuities
> in min and max?  That does seem like it could be a problem
> in the constraining transform:
>
>   real scale_xi(real xi, vector y, vector mu, vector sigma) {
>     vector[2] bounds;
>     real lb;
>     real ub;
>     bounds[1] = - inv(min((y - mu) ./ sigma));
>     bounds[2] = - inv(max((y - mu) ./ sigma));
>     lb = min(bounds);
>     ub = max(bounds);
>     return inv_logit(xi) * (ub - lb) + lb;
>   }
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] problems with "data frames"
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] problems with "data frames"
messages.body_plain:
> On Feb 3, 2017, at 10:41 AM, Jonah Gabry <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Friday, February 3, 2017 at 2:48:25 AM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> We're not talking about a data frame here, but
> a list, right?  Don't data frames have to be square?
>
> For rstan a list, for rstanarm preferably a data frame (although list can be made to work too, as data frames are just fancy lists). Data frames do not have to be square (if by square you mean same number of rows and columns).

I learn something new and surprising about R every day.

>
> I have no idea what Stata does.
>
> Somehow Stata is still in business despite only allowing one dataset in memory at a time!

So it's Andrew who wants the Stata-like behavior after all.

Here are three ways I see of proceeding:

I:  Define data objects in the environment

y1 <- list(a = a1, b = b1);
y2 <- list(a = a2, b = b2);

fit1 <- stan("foo.stan", data=y1);
fit2 <- stan("foo.stan", data=y2);

II:  Define data objects in the arguments

fit1 <- stan("foo.stan", data = list(a = a1, b = b1));
fit2 <- stan("foo.stan", data = list(a = a2, b = b2));

If you insist on calling only stan("foo.stan"), then you have
to do something destructive between calling the fits.

III:  Define data objects globally

# load one global data set
a <- a1;
b <- b1;
fit1 <- stan("foo.stan")

# load a second global data set
a <- a2;
b <- b2;
fit2 <- stan("foo.stan");

I would never in a gazillion years want to recommend (III).
Personally, I prefer I or II.  Michael's going further and
saying that at the point you have the y1 and y2 in the
first example, you should save them using rstan_dump or whatever
it's called so that you (a) have a record of the data you used
that's reproducible rather than the result of fiddling in
a REPL environment (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Read–eval–print_loop),
and (b) have a way of sharing data and Stan file in a way that's
portable across Stan interfaces.

> > Here's an example.  I start with this model (for simplicity I'm assuming we have a stan_logit() alias):
> >
> > stan_logit(y ~ dist + arsenic)
> > or
> > stan_logit(y ~ dist + arsenic, data="wells")
>
> Are you passing the name of a list or something here?
>
> I think that's just a typo. "wells" wouldn't work here. It should just be the object wells, which is a data frame.

This is the kind of thing where I never know what R's going to
do because of its flexibility with quotes in many situations.

- Bob

> > > alpha = mu*phi;

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] problems with "data frames"
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] problems with "data frames"
messages.body_plain:
Bob:

You keep talking about "global" things.  R has local environments.  For example, if you call Stan within a function, Stan will take the data from the local environment within the function call, not the global environment.

Here's a simple example:

foo <- function(){
  a <- 3
  print(a)
}

a <- 5
foo()

If you do the above, it will print 3, not 5.

P.S.  stan() takes data in the form of a list.  stan_glm() takes data in the form of a "data frame" (a matrix).

>> We're not talking about a data frame here, but
>> a list, right?  Don't data frames have to be square?
>>
>> For rstan a list, for rstanarm preferably a data frame (although list can be made to work too, as data frames are just fancy lists). Data frames do not have to be square (if by square you mean same number of rows and columns).
>
> I learn something new and surprising about R every day.
>
>>
>> I have no idea what Stata does.
>>
>> Somehow Stata is still in business despite only allowing one dataset in memory at a time!
>
> So it's Andrew who wants the Stata-like behavior after all.
>
> Here are three ways I see of proceeding:
>
> I:  Define data objects in the environment
>
> y1 <- list(a = a1, b = b1);
> y2 <- list(a = a2, b = b2);
>
> fit1 <- stan("foo.stan", data=y1);
> fit2 <- stan("foo.stan", data=y2);
>
>
> II:  Define data objects in the arguments
>
> fit1 <- stan("foo.stan", data = list(a = a1, b = b1));
> fit2 <- stan("foo.stan", data = list(a = a2, b = b2));
>
> If you insist on calling only stan("foo.stan"), then you have
> to do something destructive between calling the fits.
>
>
> III:  Define data objects globally
