You can  do that.  I think the 1/2 is a multiplicative
term in the derivative before you take log, so it's
just a constant and drops out.

> On Feb 19, 2017, at 11:53 AM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks, I was a little confused about what you were saying because I figured you could put the distribution on y_raw instead of y.

Yes, you can do put a distribution on y_raw instead of y.

I'm thinking we should start thinking more about priors
directly on the unconstrained scales.

>
> For the square root transformation, I got
>
>   target += -0.5 * log(sum(y));

Ah, you're right---I mistakenly dropped the multiplicative
0.5 alng with the additive one.
the multiplicative one

 log sqrt'(x) = log( 0.5 * sqrt(x)^(-0.5) )

              = log(0.5) - 0.5 * log(x)

and you can drop the first log(0.5).

- Bob

>
> On Saturday, February 18, 2017 at 6:54:40 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Positive unit vectors can be coded using:
>
> parameters {
>   simplex[K] y_raw;
>
> transformed parameters {
>   vector<lower=0>[K] y = sqrt(y_raw);
>
> You have to take the Jacobian into account if you want to put
> a distribution on y, but that's trivial for sqrt(), being
> just |sqrt'(x)|, so on the log scale in Stan dropping constants
> and vectorizing, it's just
>
>   target += -log(sum(y));
>
> though you should check my work on that.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Feb 17, 2017, at 8:30 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Actually, positive_unit_vector is _much_ easier to implement
> > than unit_vector as the half sphere is isomorphic to R^{n}.  Not
> > sure if there’s enough use cases to warrant the work to include
> > it in Stan, though.  Maybe a useful intro project for new devs.
> >
> >> On Feb 17, 2017, at 7:50 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >>
> >> +1 on the standardize function!
> >>
> >> In the early iterations I had tried non-centered parameterization for these, but not in the most recent version of the model. I have sufficient data so that there isn't much pooling going on. I calculate a lambda score using a formula in Gelman's book and it is near zero after fitting the model (I noticed that non-centered parameterization helps most when lambda is above 0.5, indicating lots of pooling).
> >>
> >> On unit_normal and standardizing: the issue with the way you present them is that the x_raw's don't get identified. As a result, the N_eff's will be near zero for those, which is not a big deal, but it is a big deal for lp__. I really like being able to use lp__ as a diagnostic. I don't typically print all the variables to the screen, just the hyperparamters and lp__. If lp__ is near zero, then at that point I would inspect what's going on with the other variables, If not, then I assume they are fine. When I was using those x_raws, I would get into a habit of ignoring the lp__, so other things could be going wrong in the model and I wouldn't realize it until much later. The only thing I could think of is if the calculation of N_eff for lp__ understands to ignore transformed variables that are not part of the final model.
> >>
> >> Also, I was very familiar with unit_vector. My point is that you can't say
> >> unit_vector<lower=0>[N] w;
> >> or some sort of
> >> positive_unit_vector[N] w;
> >>
> >> What I did in the model was enforce an approximate unit vector that was always positive (I don't think I can get it exact with this approach because I get imaginary numbers). The reason I included it is that the sign of z and the sign of w weren't identified in any way. Sometimes the model would output w>0 and some z[i] > 0 and sometimes it would output w<0 with that z[i] <0. Forcing w > 0 helped keep it identified in a way that putting priors on the mean of z could not. I got much better results when I included this constraint vs. doing the analysis with just the unit_vector. Indeed, the problem of nailing down the sign seems similar to the issue discussed in the Stan manual under "Inference under Label Switching" in the "Finite Mixtures" section. Unlike finite mixtures, you may not have the information necessary to put a prior that enforces the constraint in a more general PPCA model.
> >>
> >> A more general approach would probably to be something like below. This ensures that the largest square value is always positive. I haven't tried it yet and I don't know how well Stan would handle it, but I think it would be more useful than the positive_unit_vector above since it would allow sign identification in all these PPCA models, not just my specific case where I know all the w's are positive.
> >>
> >> parameters {
> >>      unit_vector[N] raw_w;
> >> }
> >> transformed parameters {
> >>      unit_vector[N] w;
> >>
> >>      w = raw_w;
> >>      if (abs(max(w)) < abs(min(w)))
> >>           w = -w;
> >> }
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >>
> >> On Fri, Feb 17, 2017 at 6:09 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
> >> Thanks for reporting back.  That's great to know that it lines
> >> up pretty closely in your application.
> >>
> >> Did you try non-centered parameterizations of z and w?  Not
> >> sure if it'd be better or worse.
> >>
> >> We have a unit vector type.  If you declare
> >>
> >>   unit_vector[K] x;
> >>
> >> it ensures x' * x = 1 and the default distribution is uniform
> >> over all unit vectors.
> >>
> >> The way it does it is as if we'd written it out by hand like this:
> >>
> >> parameters {
> >>   vector[K] x_raw;
> >>
> >> transformed parameters {
> >>   vector[K] x = x / dot_self(x);
> >>
> >> model {
> >>   x_raw ~ normal(0, 1);
> >>
> >> This ensures that the distribution on x is uniform over
> >> the unit vectors.  See:
> >>
> >> Marsaglia, G. (1972). Choosing a point from the surface of a sphere.
> >> The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 43(2):645–646.
> >>
> >> I'm not sure about a fully standardized type.  You might be
> >> able to construct it the way we construct the unit vector.
> >> The transform is just:
> >>
> >>   vector[K] x = (x - mean(x)) / sd(x);
> >>
> >> but it's not going to identify on the original y scale.  We
> >> really need a function standardize(x) to replace that RHS with
> >> efficient analytic derivatives.
> >>
> >> - Bob
> >>
> >>
> >> > On Feb 17, 2017, at 5:48 PM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >> >
> >> > I have finally got to something that fits my data with reasonable N_eff using NUTS (300 of 1000 for lp__, 1000 of 1000 for all hyperparameters, rhats between 1 and 1.01) and thought I would share (below). ADVI also fits it reasonably well. Of the hyperparameters, sd_z was higher than NUTS and the standard deviations of mu_z and sd_z were bigger than NUTS. But overall, it looks like it fits it well.
> >> >
> >> > As many folks have noted, identification is very important for these PPCA-like models. What I really needed was a way to constrain w to be a positive unit normal vector. This isn't in Stan. However, I was able to make a close enough approximation by noting that var(w) should equal 1/N - mean(w)^2 for all unit vectors. The approach I took below uses this formula to constrain the mean. Since I didn't mind that w>0, it worked out pretty well. I also put a reasonably strong prior on the standard deviation of w, combined with constraints so mean(w) didn't have any imaginary variables in it.
> >> >
> >> > Another thing I tried was to constrain z to have mean of 0 AND standard deviation of 1. The Stan documentation does a good job explaining how to force mean of 0, but it's harder than you would think to also force standard deviation of 1 while having the whole thing be identified properly (The only way I was able to do it resulted in lp__ near zero because the raw z values were not identified. The approach usually fit the data well, but it can be hard to diagnose problems when you're not printing all the variables). I tried holding back a second data point and did the math so that it works out, but it's very easy to get imaginary terms that screw it all up. So I gave up on that.
> >> >
> >> > I would really love if Stan had better support for these kinds of constraints. Positive unit vectors seems do-able, but I don't know about forced unit normals.
> >> >
> >> > data {
> >> >     int<lower=0> T;
> >> >     int<lower=0> N;
> >> >     vector[T] x[N];
> >> > }
> >> > transformed data {
> >> >     real<lower=0> one_over_N;
> >> >     real<lower=0> one_over_square_root_N;
> >> >     real<lower=0> sd_w_prior;
> >> >
> >> >     one_over_N = 1.0 / N;
> >> >     one_over_square_root_N = sqrt(one_over_N);
> >> >     sd_w_prior = 1 / (sqrt(2 * N) * inv_Phi(0.95)); //selected so 95% of
> >> >                                                     //distribution is below
> >> >                                                     //(1 / sqrt(N))
> >> > }
> >> > parameters {
> >> >     real mu_z;
> >> >     real<lower=0> sd_z;
> >> >     vector[T] z;
> >> >     real<lower=0, upper=one_over_square_root_N> sd_w;
> >> >     vector<lower=0, upper=1>[N] w;
> >> >     real<lower=0> sd_e;
> >> > }
> >> > transformed parameters {
> >> >     real<lower=0, upper=one_over_square_root_N> mu_w;
> >> >
> >> >     mu_w = sqrt(one_over_N - square(sd_w));
> >> > }
> >> > model {
> >> >     mu_z ~ normal(0, 0.5);
> >> >     sd_z ~ normal(1, 0.5);
> >> >     z ~ normal(mu_z, sd_z);
> >> >     sd_w ~ normal(0, sd_w_prior);
> >> >     w ~ normal(mu_w, sd_w);
> >> >     sd_e ~ normal(0, 0.05);
> >> >
> >> >     for (n in 1:N)
> >> >         x[n] ~ normal(z * w[n], sd_e);
> >> > }
> >> >
> >> > On Wednesday, February 15, 2017 at 2:10:41 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> >> >
> >> > > On Feb 15, 2017, at 11:44 AM, John Hall <john.mic...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >> > >
> >> > > If this is a problem for the model I posted above, then it is also a problem for the PPCA/ARD model in Figure 23 in the ADVI paper.
> >> >
> >> > Correct.
> >> >
> >> > I'm looking at the most recent incarnation of that paper, a
> >> > draft submitted (?) to JMLR (always hard to tell when authors
> >> > put preprints in the format of a journal):
> >> >
> >> > http://www.stat.columbia.edu/~gelman/research/unpublished/advi_journal.pdf
> >> >
> >> > I also wouldn't recommend the models in that paper --- they don't follow
> >> > our prior recommendations or our parameterization recommendations,
> >> > despite Andrew's being listed as a co-author.  I'm also amused that it
> >> > uses the term "automatic relevance determination", because Andrew objects
> >> > every time it's used in his presence.
> >> >
> >> > > I just ran NUTS on that exact model with my simulated data. With M=1, I got 2 / 1000 effective samples for the alpha and lp__ parameters (rhats around 10). With M=2, I got 2 / 1000 for both alphas (and rhats > 10), but a reasonable number for lp__.
> >> >
> >> > Might this be a label-switching problem?  I don't
> >> > know what PPCA/ARD is, but if it's some kind of factor
> >> > model, then that can be an issue.
> >> >
> >> > > I take your point about really strong correlations and weak identification seriously. I had realized that this was the problem with fitting the model with NUTS. The problem is that z and w in the Figure 23 model are correlated.
> >> > >
> >> > > I had assumed ADVI would be better able to handle this type of problem, especially since I knew that my model was essentially the same as what was in the paper and the paper was using this as a potential use-case of ADVI.
> >> >
> >> > Be careful what the paper evaluates.  Like most machine learning
> >> > papers, it's focused on prediction, not parameter estimation and
> >> > posterior uncertainty calibration.  Some of the earlier plots show
> >> > how these things go wrong in simple cases (like figure 5) and right
> >> > in others (at least w.r.t. the posterior mean---we know the posterior
> >> > variance is underestimated by construction of the KL divergence measure
> >> > being optimized).
> >> >
> >> > They do the predictive accuracy properly, using full Bayes for sampling
> >> > and approximate Bayes through ADVI for VI.
> >> >
> >> > - Bob

Many thanks for the discussion Bob ! I'll work on all of that. I realize that a lot of the difficulty I have encountered are due to the fact I try to apply a Frequentist simulation scheme for a Bayesian one.

On Saturday, February 18, 2017 at 2:11:50 AM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
>
> > On Feb 16, 2017, at 7:03 PM, Pierre Lebrun <lebrun...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hi Bob,
> >
> > Thanks for your answer. That's true that I don't simulate from my Bayesian model, but from a much simpler generative Normal model with no prior involved. I wouldn't have think about that ! But then it also means that the simple linear model is poorly adapted to the data, even if the generative model doesn't look different (I am just creating a line and then add some variability around).
>
> The generative model does look different.  The generative model defines
> a density over the parameters, and that's what's different.  It may feel
> similar, but what you're seeing is real differences.
>
> And you're right---the simple linear regression may not be well adapted
> to your data.  The model's definitely misspecified in the technical sense
> if it doesn't match the data-generating process, so all the guarantees
> about coverage go out the window.  This means in practice you have to be more
> careful validating on held out data to try to evaluate the sensitivity to
> this misspecification (same way as you evaluate sensitivity to priors).
> We like to use predictive posterior distributions.
>
> > What I get here that if there is a very few data points, some weakly uninformative prior should really be set to get better posteriors, but I feel that's weird to do that in a simulation setting (here, data does not represent anything, so I would need to create the prior from the data, which I won't do !).
>
> The data are supposed to represent what results from the generative
> model you specify.  The priors indicate the range the parameters can
> take.  If your inclination is to simulate from a narrow range and
> have a prior that's huge relative to that narrow range of expected
> or reasonable values, I'd suggest tightening your priors.
>
> > Prior sensitivity here is huge, and this is not something I like or is easy to deal with, in many situations.
>
> You may not like it, but if you don't have data, you can't infer from
> thin air.  If you only have a handful of data points, you want the
> prior to contribute heavily in a hierarchical model to pull your estimate
> toward a population mean (there are two case studies on the web site
> from the documentation page on hierarchical models and why you want
> to do this).
>
> >
> > On a side, when I mentioned uniform prior, I meant that I just specified a positive support for the variance/sd parameter, and no upper bound, in the parameter block, and no further proper or improper distribution.
>
> That's improper.  Meaning that it doesn't integrate to a finite value.
> Stan requires the posterior to be proper.  But if the prior is
> very wide, you need more data to get a well-behaved posterior.  Michael's
> about to roll out a case study explaining this.
>
> > And when I said the word "stabilized", I meant that the posteriors were looking more as I would expect (that was a very poor wording from my side, sorry).
>
> That's fine---that's what I thought you meant.  I don't think there's
> a good noun for that.  But it's part of the modeling process.  You want
> to make sure you're getting reasonable posteriors.
>
>
> > Weird that you cannot see the files in the first post of the thread, they have very large icons within the text in the bottom. Maybe google group is messing something on your browser... I reattached the most important file here. If you have further advice on it, I am willing to take them :-)
>
> Got it.  The key part is the model:
>
> data {
> int<lower=1> N;  // total number of observations
> vector[N] Y;  // response variable
> int<lower=1> K;  // number of population-level effects
> matrix[N, K] X;  // population-level design matrix
> }
> parameters {
> vector[K] b;  // population-level effects
> real<lower=0> sigma;  // residual SD
> }
> model {
> vector[N] eta;
> eta = X * b;
> // likelihood contribution
> Y ~ normal(eta, sigma);
> }
>
> I'd recommend indenting, but otherwise this is just a standard linear
> regression with improper flat priors on coefficients and noise scale.
>
> You may want to try simulating data and running maximum likelihood estimates
> with something like lm() in R (essentially a bootstrap estimate of the variance
> in the MLE).
>
> - Bob
>

messages.body_plain:
All stan's users,

In the manual, it was written for transforming log uniform(s|1,T)  as below :

log_unif = -log(T)

messages.subject: Random-variable objects; functions to grab posterior means, medians, sds, and mad_sd's from stan objects; also more general versions of these ideas
messages.subject_clean: Random-variable objects; functions to grab posterior means, medians, sds, and mad_sd's from stan objects; also more general versions of these ideas
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I have a few questions/requests which are relevant for my applied work, and also for the new book with Jennifer.

1.  Random-variable objects.

After I've fit a model, I'll often want to do things with the parameters.  For example, MRP.  I do it in R.  But it's awkward to work with posterior simulations in R for all the usual reasons:  I'm continually having to wrestle with array algebra, having to decide what to do with indexes.  For example, if I want to draw from normal(X*beta, sigma), I need to either figure out some slick "apply" thing or else loop on simulation draws and use indexing like beta[s,] and sigma[s], which also required me first assigning a blank object to whatever I'm creating.  Yes, it can be done, but it turns simple statistical manipulations, which would be short one-liners with random variable objects, into mini-programs.  This is, I think, contrary to the spirit both of R and of probabilistic programming.

In Stan, we can work with random variables in the generated quantities block.  But right now you can't run a generated quantities block on its own.  I think this should change:  we should allow the user to pass a stanfit object (or whatever this is called outside of R, umm, I guess it's just "the output from a fitted Stan model") and run a generated quantities block all on its own.

I suppose the alternative would be to do this using Stan functions but then we'd need a workflow for that.  Right now I find it more difficult to write a function than to write a generated quantities block, but maybe that would change with practice.

The real point is that I'd like to do math operations with random variables, and Stan seems like the right language to do this in.  Ten years ago, Jouni programmed random-variable objects in R, but as of now that does not seem like the right way to go, because (a) R is clunky, and (b) now we already have Stan which does this.

>From a Stan perspective, this is also good stuff because it's making use of Stan's capability of being a programming language (rather than the usual thing, which is that people think of Stan as a graphical modeling language, even though it isn't).  Anyway, this would be a big help both for applied work and for teaching / textbook writing.

2.  Stan output.

Currently, in addition to Rhat and n_eff, we report posterior mean, sd, and a bunch of quantiles.  I'm wondering if we should follow the model of rstanarm and replace mean and sd by median and mad_sd (that's the median absolute deviation from the median, multiplied by a scaling factor so that it is equivalent to the sd for the case of the normal distribution).  These have the advantage that they always exist (so will work, for example, with the Cauchy distribution), also I think they're closer to what users should really want in most applications.  Similarly, we'd replace se_mean by mad_se which is just mad_sd/sqrt(n_eff).  Then for the quantiles, now we report 2.5%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 97.5%.  OK, we don't need 50% anymore.  I'd recommend removing 2.5% and 97.5% too (or maybe not, I'm not quite sure; on one hand, focusing on these intervals is bad practice, and these tail values have lots of simulation noise; on the other, it can be good for people to see some wide uncertainty bounds).

So here's the new output:

median mad_sd 25% 75% n_eff mad_se Rhat

You can see that I changed the order a bit.  I find se_mean (or, equivalently, mad_se) a bit difficult to explain.  I end up just saying it's sd/sqrt(n_eff) (or mad_sd/sqrt(n_eff), but, if so, it makes sense for it to appear _after_ n_eff in the table.  Finally, I kept Rhat at the end because it's convenient to scan the output and look at R_hat.

3.  Pulling out parameter estimates:

Suppose I want to just grab point estimates and se's from a stanfit object in R.  I can do something like this:
beta_hat <- summary(fit, pars="beta")$summary$mean
(Actually I'd prefer median but that's no big deal right now.)
But the above is quite a mouthful.
Also, if beta is a matrix or array of 2 or more dimensions, I'd like to be able to automatically grab the estimates in matrix or array form, which the above won't do for me.

Or I could do it directly from the Stan output, but that involves looping or figuring out apply() and also doesn't easily generalize beyond scalars and 1-way arrays.

I _think_ what I'm looking for is a function such as posterior_mean(fit, pars="beta")) which returns an object the same size and shape as beta, or maybe something like posterior_mean(fit, pars=c("alpha,"beta","gamma")) which returns a list.

Another way would be something like this:  posterior_summary(fit, pars, f), which would apply the function "f" to the parameter or parameters in "pars".  For example, posterior_summary(fit, "beta", median) or posterior_summary(fit, c("alpha","beta"), mad).

Hmmm, now I'm thinking that this idea could get us in the direction of working with random variables!  For example, what about this sort of function:

posterior_computation(fit, f, data_args, rv_args).  Here, "f" is a user-supplied function and it is applied to the stanfit object "fit", along with optional arguments "data_args" and "rv_args".  The "data_args" are data supplied to the "foo" function; the "rv_args" are also supplied to "foo" but as random variable objects, meaning that they are grabbed one simulation draw at a time).  For example:
foo <- function(X, beta, sigma) {y_hat <- X%*%beta; N <- length(y_hat); return(rnorm(N, y_hat, sigma))};
sims <- posterior_computation(fit, foo, data_args=X_new)
If "foo" returns an array of dimensions "dim_foo", then sims will be an array of dimensions (n_sims, dim_foo), where n_sims is the number of simulations in the stanfit object "fit".

The above will not work in complete generality because I was assuming that "foo" would return an array of fixed dimension (so that they can be put together in one big array that's one dimension higher).  But in general "foo" could return anything.  So I guess that in general, posterior_computation() would have to return a list of length n_sims.  Such a list would be more awkward to work with so maybe there could be an option to collapse it back into an array if all the elements in the list are scalars or else arrays of identical size and shape.

Also we'd want these all to work for stanreg objects but that should be easy enough, I assume, as stanreg objects are themselves the output of stan fits, with some extra information.

4.  Summary

In rstan, I'd like to see these new functions (or maybe they exist already?):

posterior_summary(fit, pars, function)
posterior_computation(fit, function, data_args, rv_args)
and some sort of collapsing function for random variable lists.

It would also be good to be able to do more of this in Stan, using the generated quantities block (or maybe using functions but then I need a clean workflow for this in R).

Any thoughts?

messages.body_plain:
I'm not sure this solves all of Andrew's wish-list, but I recently created a few helper functions to ease the workflow for regression-like models at least.

Attached is the code, which first has a special contrast matrix function that wraps model.matrix but additionally stores the data as an attribute of the resulting matrix, that you would use as:

  X = get_contrast_matrix(
  data = my_data
  , formula = ~ age * sex
  )

Then a function to use this matrix plus the stan_fit to work out posterior predictions on the conditions of the experiment (assumes the model was fit with the matrix form of regression as on pg 121 of the manual):

  conditions = get_condition_post(
    post = post_from_stan
    , par = 'beta'
    , X = X
  )

Which you can then work with in a standard dplyr chain, for example:

  conditions %>%
    group_by(
        age
        , sex
    ) %>%
    summarize(
        med = median(value)
        , lo95 = quantile(value,.025)
        , lo50 = quantile(value,.25)
        , hi50 = quantile(value,.75)
        , lo95 = quantile(value,.975)
    )

--
Mike Lawrence
Graduate Student
Department of Psychology & Neuroscience
Dalhousie University

~ Certainty is (possibly) folly ~

messages.body_plain:
It’s fine if you want to add MAD, although I don’t find it as useful, but
we absolutely cannot remove mean and mcmc_se as these are the
only theoretically-meaningful outputs of the Markov chains.  There is,
for example, no CLT for mad_d/sqrt(n_eff).  You could strain and
find something sort of similar but it would have some exceptional
behavior making things awkward.

2.5% and 97.5%, however, should definitely go.

> On Feb 20, 2017, at 7:04 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>

> 2.  Stan output.
>
> Currently, in addition to Rhat and n_eff, we report posterior mean, sd, and a bunch of quantiles.  I'm wondering if we should follow the model of rstanarm and replace mean and sd by median and mad_sd (that's the median absolute deviation from the median, multiplied by a scaling factor so that it is equivalent to the sd for the case of the normal distribution).  These have the advantage that they always exist (so will work, for example, with the Cauchy distribution), also I think they're closer to what users should really want in most applications.  Similarly, we'd replace se_mean by mad_se which is just mad_sd/sqrt(n_eff). Then for the quantiles, now we report 2.5%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 97.5%.  OK, we don't need 50% anymore.  I'd recommend removing 2.5% and 97.5% too (or maybe not, I'm not quite sure; on one hand, focusing on these intervals is bad practice, and these tail values have lots of simulation noise; on the other, it can be good for people to see some wide uncertainty bounds).
>
> So here's the new output:
>
> median mad_sd 25% 75% n_eff mad_se Rhat
>
> You can see that I changed the order a bit.  I find se_mean (or, equivalently, mad_se) a bit difficult to explain.  I end up just saying it's sd/sqrt(n_eff) (or mad_sd/sqrt(n_eff), but, if so, it makes sense for it to appear _after_ n_eff in the table.  Finally, I kept Rhat at the end because it's convenient to scan the output and look at R_hat.

messages.subject: Further strategies to deal with divergent transitions
messages.subject_clean: Further strategies to deal with divergent transitions
messages.body_plain:
Hi there! First of all, thank you for being awesome. I enjoy programming in Stan A LOT and I always read this mailing list hoping to learn something new.

I've got this little model full of divergent transitions. It's a GARCH(1, 1) model (as implemented in the manual) for K = 2 states where the transition probabilities are estimated by the forward algorithm. On a single run, the code estimates the parameters for n = 1, ..., N independent datasets. Please, find attached my fully working code and an output summary so you don't have to run it yourself. The estimates make sense at first glance, but I was warned that they are biased. As stated by Intergalactic Betan Policies, they shouldn't be trusted. I first thought the sampler is having a hard time at estimating parameters for N independent datasets, but I made the model collapse to N = 1 and had the same problem. Also, I'd like to keep everything together so I can add some hierarchical magic later.

After long reading this mailing list, I've learnt my posterior is misbehaved and the sampler walks clumsily along the curvature, taking steps so big it won't discover the details of the surface. Usually, three strategies are discussed: (1) force the sampling take smaller steps by increasing adapt_delta and decreasing stepsize, (2) add prior information to smooth the posterior curvature, and (3) reparametrise. The first step will help mostly with divergences on the upper diagonal of the pairs plot. In my case, it solved part of the problem, leaving 250/1600 divergences when adapt_delta = 0.99 and stepsize = 0.01. For step two, unfortunately I don't have many parameters in my models. Even more, most them are highly constrained (namely 0 < alpha1 <= 1, beta1 => 0, alpha1+beta1 < 1, p0 and TP are probabilities with 0 <= p <= 1). Basically, there's not much room for priors. For the last step, well, my model is pretty simple so I don't know how to reparametrise this prima facie.

Being stuck, I can only send the distress signal and ask the savvy what other strategies you'd suggest. Do you see something suspicious in my code? Maybe some snippet that smells bad? S.O.S.

Regards,

Luis.

I'm trying to estimate a large latent variable model using RStan. I'm getting several divergent transitions after warmup when performing estimation on simulated data and am trying to diagnose the problem using pairs() plots.

I've looked at scatterplots between each parameter and lp__ using the pairs() function. Most divergent transitions occur below the diagonal, suggesting that the model needs to be reparameterized. messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] What to look for in pairs() diagnostic plots?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] What to look for in pairs() diagnostic plots?
messages.body_plain:
The pairs plot by default sets up two chains above the diagonal
and two chains below the diagonal.  So all this is saying is that
they're happening on a subset of the chains.  You want to see where
the divergences are at to see if you can learn anything.

The ideal pairs plot will look like a bunch of bulls-eyes of
independent unit-scaled posteriors.  Anything that smacks of high
correlation or varying scales can be a problem for adaptation or
sampling.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Because

  uniform(y | a, b) = 1 / (b - a)

so

  log uniform(y | a, b) = -log(b - a)

so

  log uniform(y | 0, T) = -log(T)

Doesn't matter how small (b - a) is.

Because

  uniform(y | a, b) = 1 / (b - a)

so

  log uniform(y | a, b) = -log(b - a)

so

Doesn't matter how small (b - a) is.

Cool.  Thanks.  Stan needs a lot of memory to compile models, but
not nearly as much memory to run models.  If you run in CmdStan rather
than R, the draws are streamed out and that really cuts down on the
amount of memory you need at run time.

So if you're using something like RStanArm, which pre-builds models,
then you should be able to get away with a smaller instance.  You
might be able to do the same packaging in AWS.

messages.body_plain:
> On Feb 20, 2017, at 7:04 AM, Andrew Gelman <Gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
>
> Hi, I have a few questions/requests which are relevant for my applied work, and also for the new book with Jennifer.
>
> 1.  Random-variable objects.
>
> After I've fit a model, I'll often want to do things with the parameters.  For example, MRP.  I do it in R.  But it's awkward to work with posterior simulations in R for all the usual reasons:  I'm continually having to wrestle with array algebra, having to decide what to do with indexes.  For example, if I want to draw from normal(X*beta, sigma), I need to either figure out some slick "apply" thing or else loop on simulation draws and use indexing like beta[s,] and sigma[s], which also required me first assigning a blank object to whatever I'm creating.  Yes, it can be done, but it turns simple statistical manipulations, which would be short one-liners with random variable objects, into mini-programs.  This is, I think, contrary to the spirit both of R and of probabilistic programming.

To code this up and R, you'd need to reimplement all the functions you want
to work with random variable data types.  This is what that package with Jouni.

> In Stan, we can work with random variables in the generated quantities block.  But right now you can't run a generated quantities block on its own.  I think this should change:  we should allow the user to pass a stanfit object (or whatever this is called outside of R, umm, I guess it's just "the output from a fitted Stan model") and run a generated quantities block all on its own.

Yes.  Everyone agrees this is a good feature.  We'll add it
pretty soon, but not in 2.15---that's going to be just getting
the refactor into production.

Just need to get the round trip of converting outputs into
initializations.

...

> 2.  Stan output.
>
> Currently, in addition to Rhat and n_eff, we report posterior mean, sd, and a bunch of quantiles.  I'm wondering if we should follow the model of rstanarm and replace mean and sd by median and mad_sd (that's the median absolute deviation from the median, multiplied by a scaling factor so that it is equivalent to the sd for the case of the normal distribution).

That sounds too complicated to me.  I always think of these things
in terms of how we want to document it.

> These have the advantage that they always exist (so will work, for example, with the Cauchy distribution), also I think they're closer to what users should really want in most applications.  Similarly, we'd replace se_mean by mad_se which is just mad_sd/sqrt(n_eff).  Then for the quantiles, now we report 2.5%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 97.5%.  OK, we don't need 50% anymore.  I'd recommend removing 2.5% and 97.5% too (or maybe not, I'm not quite sure; on one hand, focusing on these intervals is bad practice, and these tail values have lots of simulation noise; on the other, it can be good for people to see some wide uncertainty bounds).
>
> So here's the new output:
>
> median mad_sd 25% 75% n_eff mad_se Rhat

Are you going to stop using means altogether?  I think there'd
be a user revolt if we don't have mean and se_mean (though I'll
admit users get confused between se_mean and posterior sd).

> You can see that I changed the order a bit.  I find se_mean (or, equivalently, mad_se) a bit difficult to explain.

>  I end up just saying it's sd/sqrt(n_eff)

That seems pretty easy to me.

> (or mad_sd/sqrt(n_eff), but, if so, it makes sense for it to appear _after_ n_eff in the table.  Finally, I kept Rhat at the end because it's convenient to scan the output and look at R_hat.

I don't mind the order.

> 3.  Pulling out parameter estimates:

I'll leave this up to the RStan devs.  I don't have problems with
this the way things are, but can see how it could be streamlined
for some common operations.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Hi Bob!

Thanks for you answer. You are right in that I was actually referring to posterior std-dev and not MC error.

So I have J patients for which I integrate an ODE. All patients have the exact same parameter set.

For J=6 the posterior std-dev of the parameter of interest is of the order of 1E-2 and the usual sampler parameters look fine:

> sp6 <- get_sampler_params(res[["6"]], inc_warmup=FALSE)[[1]]
> colMeans(sp6)
accept_stat__    stepsize__   treedepth__  n_leapfrog__   divergent__
   0.90502219    0.02050799    3.60000000   18.52000000    0.00000000
     energy__
 407.13425909

Now, when I go to J=8, then I run the same number of iterations, yes (75 warmup and 50 post-warmup), but now things break seriously. The run takes 2H, nothing converges at all and the posterior sd is of the order of 1E-12! The sampler did go completely insane:

> sp8 <- get_sampler_params(res[["8"]], inc_warmup=FALSE)[[1]]
> colMeans(sp8)
accept_stat__    stepsize__   treedepth__  n_leapfrog__   divergent__
 1.001197e-01  5.093111e-16  1.000000e+01  1.023000e+03  0.000000e+00
     energy__
 1.230724e+03

So the stepsize got reduced to essentially 0, the treedepth is maxed out and we take 1023 leapfrog steps on average.

I think the reason is the limited accuracy of the ODE integrator here which somehow defeats NUTS. I do find this somewhat worrysome, as I thought that a robust numerical procedure should be able to cope with limited precision and simply output a result with limited precision. Anything else I can look into which helps?

Best,
Sebastian

I do so in a very simple way in that there is no between-subject variability and I provide Stan with a lot of data. Once I go to 8 patients then the running time explodes to 2h and the estimates are just crap.

Agreed.  This will be a key principle in our methodology guides.
We've been learning a lot of this ourselves as we go.  Michael's

> Certainly, it's a technical manual and not a handbook, but that's a very, very intuitive rule to guide the modelling process: try to make all the parameters standarized and uncorrelated.

The Stan manual's going to be split into two parts:

1.  the reference manual with the language spec and the functions doc

> Maybe too obvios, but it's worth noting this is true for actual parameters to be estimated and not for transformed parameters, right?

Correct.  Keep in mind that's on the unconstrained scale,
not the constrained scale.  So if you have a parameter with
<lower = 0>, it's the log of the parameter.  If you have
a covariance matrix, it's the Cholesky factor with log-transformed
diagonal.  Unfortunately, you can't access that directly through

messages.body_plain:
On Monday, February 20, 2017 at 1:16:42 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> The pairs plot by default sets up two chains above the diagonal
> and two chains below the diagonal.  So all this is saying is that
> they're happening on a subset of the chains.  You want to see where
> the divergences are at to see if you can learn anything.

This hasn't been true for a couple of years. By default, the draws (across all chains) with below median accept_stat__ are below the diagonal and those with above median accept_stat__ are above the diagonal. If there are divergent transitions above the diagonal, those can usually be fixed with a higher adapt_delta. If they are below the diagonal, you can try increasing adapt_delta but oftentimes you have to adjust the model.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] can we limit the targeted MC error despite much data?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] can we limit the targeted MC error despite much data?
messages.body_plain:
I don’t know what you expect NUTS, or any algorithm, to do.
When the ODE solver starts returning inaccurate gradients
then the Hamiltonian transitions are poor and the acceptance
probability plummets.  All NUTS can do is reject these poor
proposals and stay at the initial point, which the adaptation
tries to improve by decreasing the step size.  If the error
wasn’t due to the HMC integrator but systematic bias from
the ODE integrator then this won’t help and you end up in
a bad state.

And this is all a good outcome compared to what could
potentially happen if not only the gradients were bad but
also the log density calculations were also biased in which
case the acceptance procedure wouldn’t work and you’d
end up with biased chains.

Personally I’d look at the quality of the data that you’re using.
Misfit can push the parameters into places where the ODE
integrator stumbles.  It’s highly unlikely that adding new
patients will cause the posterior to collapse to pathological
parameter values that the posterior somehow missed before.

> On Feb 20, 2017, at 3:49 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:

>     0.9245461     0.0152286     4.0800000    33.2400000     0.0000000
>      energy__
>   541.3679865
> >
>
> So it looks like the limited ODE precision is the problem here. Can I expect NUTS to deal with the limited precision? It obviously doesn't, but I am not sure if increasing the precision is a game I can always play.
>
> I can probably now find again a sample size at which I break things at the fixed 1E-14 precision.
>
> Sebastian
>

> > >

> > >      energy__

> > >      energy__

I do find this somewhat worrysome, as I thought that a robust numerical procedure should be able to cope with limited precision and simply output a result with limited precision. Anything else I can look into which helps?

> > > >
> > > > Hi!
> > > >
> > > > I have encountered the bizarre situation that with increasing the sample size of my fake data simulation the computation time explodes discontinuously at some point and convergence of the parameter estimates vanishes suddenly.
> > > >
> > > > I am simulating a number of patients using an ODE and then try to recover the parameters. I do so in a very simple way in that there is no between-subject variability and I provide Stan with a lot of data. What happens is when I run this with 4 or 6 patients, then everything is fine (running time is 61s and 75s / estimates are as simulated). Once I go to 8 patients then the running time explodes to 2h and the estimates are just crap.
> > > >

That is, I provide so much data that the MC error is below the 1E-7 which effectively renders the HMC sampler blind given the precision the data likelihood would provide. So I endup in the bizarre situation that more data kills my Stan run due to the limited ODE precision. What can be done about this? The obvious answer is to increase the ODE precision, but that is a limited game. Can we somehow force Stan to run the sampler with a limited precision? I mean, I don't mind in this situation iof the answer from the sampler is not as precise as the data would allow me to make inferences. However, I would really appreciate an answer in such a situation, but with an artificially more unprecise result - that would be much better than no answer at all.

messages.subject: Vectorization and non-centered parameterization with nested groups
messages.subject_clean: Vectorization and non-centered parameterization with nested groups
messages.body_plain:
Hi Stan users,

I’m trying to fit a hierarchical binomial-logit model with nested groups and am having some problems with vectorizing and implementing the the non-centered parameterization.

I’m working my way up to a more complex model, but to illustrate my problem I'll use an example of the effect of county-level healthcare funding on case-fatality rates. There is nesting as observations are reported from counties, which are nested within states. Each observation (row) indicates the number of deaths and a total number of cases, with multiple observations per county. In this case there is a small number of states (5).

First off, I was trying to use a vectorized non-centered parameterization, with the state and county effects in vectorized form in the transformed parameters block. However, I get divergent transitions which cannot be alleviated by increasing adapt delta. This plagued me for quite a while until I found a note from Bob saying that intermediate levels cannot (yet) be vectorized in Stan (http://stackoverflow.com/questions/29379001/nested-model-in-stan).

So then I tried a looped and centered version following his example, which included moving the state and county effects into the model block.

This works (great!) but now that I’m attempting to implement the non-centered parameterization, I again get divergent transitions and I’m not sure why.

Any help to figure out the problem, or pointers on correct syntax for non-centered parameterizations with multiply nested groups would be greatly appreciated!

Attached is code to simulate data, as well as the three models. This is my first Stan model so I apologize if I’m making any obvious mistakes.

Max

P.S. I'm running Rstan 2.14.1

messages.body_plain:
I've encountered this situation from time to time over the years.  One thing that sometimes works is a parameterization of the form, sd = sigma*(E(y)/Z)^alpha, where A is a constant set so that the thing inside the exponent is of order 1, and alpha is restricted to (0,1).  Another thing is to try modeling everything on the log scale.  Another tip is to use informative priors for the sigmas.  Another tip is to set up the parameterization so the sigmas are on unit scale.  In your example you can replace mu^2 by (mu/A)^2.

Hey, I guess this should go into the priors wiki!

A

I know this is a constructed exampled which may not be relevant for applications; however, I cannot exclude this from being relevant at this point.

My (user) expectation in this case would be a warning of possibly imprecise gradients and a possibly slightly biased solution. I would be much happier with a result given to me with a warning rather than no result at all. If NUTS could just produce a less accurate, but a still valid result (under the assumption that the truncation error is bias free) - that would be the perfect solution if that's possible.

>From what you raised could these workarounds help (or how would they fail):

- Lowering the targeted acceptance rate to 60% or so should allow the Hamiltonian flow to be not that accurate and could solve the issue here, right? Things would not run efficient, but they would run at least.

- How about introducing a minimal step-size? This would limit the acceptance probability whenever that minimal step-size is hit, but again things would keep running, just not as efficient.

- Running things with a fixed step-size, so using vanilla HMC may work as well, right?

I guess that the main concern with the above options is potential bias which is uncontrolled. However, no answer at all is not very satisfactory for a user; rather an answer with a fat warning would be preferable - at least to me.

Sebastian

messages.subject_clean: double exponential
messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, February 21, 2017 at 11:12:23 AM UTC-5, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> Thanks! I was looking for that as I remembered this was mentioned somewhere, but I did not find the right "google words".
>
> Would it make sense to use what rstanarm has done also for the double exponential distribution definition in stan::math?

I don't think so. The function in the Stan Math library does what it is supposed to do, but when used in conjunction with NUTS, it can lead to poor MCMC estimates when the leapfrogger leaps over the discontinuity at zero. In a Stan program, you can introduce the scale-mixture parameter in the parameters block, define the thing that is supposed have a Laplace prior in transformed parameters, and then ignore the margins of the output that you do not care about.

Ben

messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

I often look at n_eff samples in the summary report. I reparameterize where the n_eff is low or change the distribution, from cauchy to student-t with nu = 4.
Sometimes I use the inv_gamma distribution (but I fit the range values with fitdistrplus) R-package and give some extra to the variance.
Sometimes applying the MATT trick does help too. I never figured out however, why there is this problem in my models.
Thus I felt modeling is an art not only a science.

Andre

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: double exponential
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Re: double exponential
messages.body_plain:
Right --- we can't do sampling inside our function definition!

We could, though, define variables with built-in priors:

  normal_real<mu, sigma> y;

and have that be equivalent to putting this in the parameters block

  normal y;

and

  y ~ normal(mu, sigma);

in the model block.  Then all of a sudden our models would look
a lot more like other probabilistic programs.  Like Michael, I'm
not convinced this kind of thing is a good idea.

- Bob

On Feb 21, 2017, at 11:27 AM, Ben Goodrich <goodri...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> On Tuesday, February 21, 2017 at 11:12:23 AM UTC-5, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> Thanks! I was looking for that as I remembered this was mentioned somewhere, but I did not find the right "google words".
>
> Would it make sense to use what rstanarm has done also for the double exponential distribution definition in stan::math?
>
> I don't think so. The function in the Stan Math library does what it is supposed to do, but when used in conjunction with NUTS, it can lead to poor MCMC estimates when the leapfrogger leaps over the discontinuity at zero. In a Stan program, you can introduce the scale-mixture parameter in the parameters block, define the thing that is supposed have a Laplace prior in transformed parameters, and then ignore the margins of the output that you do not care about.
>
> Ben
>

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] can we limit the targeted MC error despite much data?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] can we limit the targeted MC error despite much data?
messages.body_plain:
For reference: Playing a bit with the adapt_delta parameter indeed works as I expected. That is, reducing adapt_delta to values below the default of 0.9 in rstan made things work again (at the initial precision of 1E-10). Going a bit further showed that when going to even lower adapt_delta of 0.6 results in some nice speedups. The chosen stepsize increases as expected. However, when turning it too low, then things fall apart.

I am aware of the common recommendation to use high adapt_delta values. I wonder if this recommendation still holds when we have to deal with low-precision gradients as it happens when dealing with ODEs where it is super-expensive to get very high precision. The price one will probably pay is not being able to deal with complicated posterior geometry...but nothing is free.

Sebastian

On Tuesday, February 21, 2017 at 9:12:52 AM UTC+1, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> Thanks Mike.
>
> I know this is a constructed exampled which may not be relevant for applications; however, I cannot exclude this from being relevant at this point.
>
> My (user) expectation in this case would be a warning of possibly imprecise gradients and a possibly slightly biased solution. I would be much happier with a result given to me with a warning rather than no result at all. If NUTS could just produce a less accurate, but a still valid result (under the assumption that the truncation error is bias free) - that would be the perfect solution if that's possible.
>
> From what you raised could these workarounds help (or how would they fail):
>
> - Lowering the targeted acceptance rate to 60% or so should allow the Hamiltonian flow to be not that accurate and could solve the issue here, right? Things would not run efficient, but they would run at least.
>
> - How about introducing a minimal step-size? This would limit the acceptance probability whenever that minimal step-size is hit, but again things would keep running, just not as efficient.
>
> - Running things with a fixed step-size, so using vanilla HMC may work as well, right?
>
> I guess that the main concern with the above options is potential bias which is uncontrolled. However, no answer at all is not very satisfactory for a user; rather an answer with a fat warning would be preferable - at least to me.
>
> Sebastian
>
> On Tuesday, February 21, 2017 at 1:39:38 AM UTC+1, Michael Betancourt wrote:
> > I don’t know what you expect NUTS, or any algorithm, to do.
> > When the ODE solver starts returning inaccurate gradients
> > then the Hamiltonian transitions are poor and the acceptance
> > probability plummets.  All NUTS can do is reject these poor
> > proposals and stay at the initial point, which the adaptation
> > tries to improve by decreasing the step size.  If the error
> > wasn’t due to the HMC integrator but systematic bias from
> > the ODE integrator then this won’t help and you end up in
> > a bad state.
> >
> > And this is all a good outcome compared to what could
> > potentially happen if not only the gradients were bad but
> > also the log density calculations were also biased in which
> > case the acceptance procedure wouldn’t work and you’d
> > end up with biased chains.
> >
> > Personally I’d look at the quality of the data that you’re using.
> > Misfit can push the parameters into places where the ODE
> > integrator stumbles.  It’s highly unlikely that adding new
> > patients will cause the posterior to collapse to pathological
> > parameter values that the posterior somehow missed before.
> >
> > > On Feb 20, 2017, at 3:49 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > That's easy, sure. Going from 1E-10 to 1E-14 for abs and rel tolerances then things work again:
> > >
> > > > colMeans(get_sampler_params(fake_run_serial, inc_warmup=FALSE)[[1]])
> > > accept_stat__    stepsize__   treedepth__  n_leapfrog__   divergent__
> > >     0.9245461     0.0152286     4.0800000    33.2400000     0.0000000
> > >      energy__
> > >   541.3679865
> > > >
> > >
> > > So it looks like the limited ODE precision is the problem here. Can I expect NUTS to deal with the limited precision? It obviously doesn't, but I am not sure if increasing the precision is a game I can always play.
> > >
> > > I can probably now find again a sample size at which I break things at the fixed 1E-14 precision.
> > >
> > > Sebastian
> > >
> > > On Monday, February 20, 2017 at 8:50:01 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > Can you increase accuracy of the ODE integrator to see if that solves
> > > > the problem?  Seems like it's an easy enough hypothesis to test, so
> > > > to speak.
> > > >
> > > > - Bob
> > > >
> > > > > On Feb 20, 2017, at 2:20 PM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > >
> > > > > Hi Bob!
> > > > >
> > > > > Thanks for you answer. You are right in that I was actually referring to posterior std-dev and not MC error.
> > > > >
> > > > > So I have J patients for which I integrate an ODE. All patients have the exact same parameter set.
> > > > >
> > > > > For J=6 the posterior std-dev of the parameter of interest is of the order of 1E-2 and the usual sampler parameters look fine:
> > > > >
> > > > > > sp6 <- get_sampler_params(res[["6"]], inc_warmup=FALSE)[[1]]
> > > > > > colMeans(sp6)
> > > > > accept_stat__    stepsize__   treedepth__  n_leapfrog__   divergent__
> > > > >    0.90502219    0.02050799    3.60000000   18.52000000    0.00000000
> > > > >      energy__
> > > > >  407.13425909
> > > > >
> > > > > Now, when I go to J=8, then I run the same number of iterations, yes (75 warmup and 50 post-warmup), but now things break seriously. The run takes 2H, nothing converges at all and the posterior sd is of the order of 1E-12! The sampler did go completely insane:
> > > > >
> > > > > > sp8 <- get_sampler_params(res[["8"]], inc_warmup=FALSE)[[1]]
> > > > > > colMeans(sp8)
> > > > > accept_stat__    stepsize__   treedepth__  n_leapfrog__   divergent__
> > > > >  1.001197e-01  5.093111e-16  1.000000e+01  1.023000e+03  0.000000e+00
> > > > >      energy__
> > > > >  1.230724e+03
> > > > >
> > > > > So the stepsize got reduced to essentially 0, the treedepth is maxed out and we take 1023 leapfrog steps on average.
> > > > >
> > > > > I think the reason is the limited accuracy of the ODE integrator here which somehow defeats NUTS. I do find this somewhat worrysome, as I thought that a robust numerical procedure should be able to cope with limited precision and simply output a result with limited precision. Anything else I can look into which helps?
> > > > >
> > > > > Best,
> > > > > Sebastian
> > > > >
> > > > > On Sunday, February 19, 2017 at 10:38:54 PM UTC+1, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> > > > > MCMC error is estimated as
> > > > >
> > > > >   posterior std-dev / sqrt(n_eff)
> > > > >
> > > > > It's not something that gets controlled directly.  Or are you
> > > > > talking about the Hamiltonian simulation error due to the leapfrog
> > > > > error?  I think that's usually minimal until you hit a divergence and
> > > > > it spins off to infinity.
> > > > >
> > > > > It still gets through as many iterations in the 2H?  Any idea if
> > > > > you're spiking memory or something and starting to swap?  Oare
> > > > > are you seeing the tree depth explode?
> > > > >
> > > > > Each of those integrate_ode calls is for an independent patient?
> > > > >
> > > > > - Bob
> > > > >
> > > > > > On Feb 19, 2017, at 8:40 AM, Sebastian Weber <sdw....@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Hi!
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I have encountered the bizarre situation that with increasing the sample size of my fake data simulation the computation time explodes discontinuously at some point and convergence of the parameter estimates vanishes suddenly.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I am simulating a number of patients using an ODE and then try to recover the parameters. I do so in a very simple way in that there is no between-subject variability and I provide Stan with a lot of data. What happens is when I run this with 4 or 6 patients, then everything is fine (running time is 61s and 75s / estimates are as simulated). Once I go to 8 patients then the running time explodes to 2h and the estimates are just crap.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > From my rough understanding the limited precision of the ODE integrator (set to 1E-10, maybe in reality 1E-7) is the problem here. That is, I provide so much data that the MC error is below the 1E-7 which effectively renders the HMC sampler blind given the precision the data likelihood would provide. So I endup in the bizarre situation that more data kills my Stan run due to the limited ODE precision. What can be done about this? The obvious answer is to increase the ODE precision, but that is a limited game. Can we somehow force Stan to run the sampler with a limited precision? I mean, I don't mind in this situation iof the answer from the sampler is not as precise as the data would allow me to make inferences. However, I would really appreciate an answer in such a situation, but with an artificially more unprecise result - that would be much better than no answer at all.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Best,
> > > > > > Sebastian

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] can we limit the targeted MC error despite much data?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] can we limit the targeted MC error despite much data?
messages.body_plain:
The difference is that the HMC error is adjusted with Metropolis.

With bad ODEs, it's not just bad gradients, but also bad solutions.
They're controlled by the same parameter.

We don't know what the cutoff is.  Obviously we're using
double-precision (64 bit) floating point in all of our calculations.
But maybe single-precision (32 bit) would be enough.  Or maybe
somewhere in between.  Double precision is about 1e-14 and
single precision about 1e-7.  Unfortunately, those are our only
two viable choices for primitive real types in C++ (until quadruple
precision becomes more common).

What is often more important is the algebra of the expressions,
such as whether subtractions lead to catastrophic cancellations.

I believe most GPUs are only optimized for single-precision, but
I'm not at all certain of that.

- Bob

> probability plummets.  All NUTS can do is reject these poor
> proposals and stay at the initial point, which the adaptation
> tries to improve by decreasing the step size.  If the error
> wasn’t due to the HMC integrator but systematic bias from
> the ODE integrator then this won’t help and you end up in
> a bad state.
>
> And this is all a good outcome compared to what could
> potentially happen if not only the gradients were bad but
> also the log density calculations were also biased in which
> case the acceptance procedure wouldn’t work and you’d
> end up with biased chains.
>
> Personally I’d look at the quality of the data that you’re using.
> Misfit can push the parameters into places where the ODE
> integrator stumbles.  It’s highly unlikely that adding new
> patients will cause the posterior to collapse to pathological
> parameter values that the posterior somehow missed before.

messages.body_plain:
> On Feb 21, 2017, at 12:25 PM, andre.pfeuffer via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
>
> Hi David,
>
> I often look at n_eff samples in the summary report. I reparameterize where the n_eff is low or change the distribution, from cauchy to student-t with nu = 4.
> Sometimes I use the inv_gamma distribution (but I fit the range values with fitdistrplus) R-package and give some extra to the variance.
> Sometimes applying the MATT trick does help too. I never figured out however, why there is this problem in my models.
> Thus I felt modeling is an art not only a science.

There are two different things going on here.

For computational efficiency and numerical stability, we'd like
the parameters to be independent in the posterior and unit scale.
Ideally without fat tails.  Unit normal works well.

Of course, we can't get that, but often we can reparameterize to
get the same inferences with a better behaved posterior.  The centered
parameterization is better when there's a lot of data and the non-centered
when there's less;  better here is looking more like a standard normal.

The other issue is the statistical aspect of the model.  Often we wind
up with posteriors that are inconsistent with our prior information.  Often
we're vague about prior information, but there's enough data to make up
for it.  When there's less data, there's much more prior sensitivity.
So we want to look at the posteriors to see if they make sense, and if
not, apply stronger priors so that the end-to-end inferences make sense.

Andrew's "folk theorem" ties these things together---misspecified models
(either in the prior or in the likelihood) are often also hard to fit.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Those aren't the same.  The run time is going to be
a factor of multiple things:

   iteration / n_eff  --- how well it mixes

   leapfrog / iteration --- how many leapfrog steps per iteration

   seconds / leapfrog --- how long the log density and gradients take

And warmup works completely differently from sampling (it's more herky-jerky
as it finds its way to an adapted state).

You can get number of leapfrog steps per iteration out of the interfaces
and do your own timing and we report n_eff.

There's variation across chains with the same model depending on
random seed for initialization and initial moves.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
The reason for using the mad_sd is that it gives roughly the "right" behavior for long-tailed distributions such as the t.  It's not a big deal but in writing the new regression book I've liked mad_sd as it's more interpretable for regressions when degrees of freedom are low.

> On Feb 20, 2017, at 8:41 AM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> It’s fine if you want to add MAD, although I don’t find it as useful, but
> we absolutely cannot remove mean and mcmc_se as these are the
> only theoretically-meaningful outputs of the Markov chains.  There is,
> for example, no CLT for mad_d/sqrt(n_eff).  You could strain and
> find something sort of similar but it would have some exceptional
> behavior making things awkward.
>
> 2.5% and 97.5%, however, should definitely go.
>
> > On Feb 20, 2017, at 7:04 AM, Andrew Gelman <gel...@stat.columbia.edu> wrote:
> >
> > 2.  Stan output.
> >
> > Currently, in addition to Rhat and n_eff, we report posterior mean, sd, and a bunch of quantiles.  I'm wondering if we should follow the model of rstanarm and replace mean and sd by median and mad_sd (that's the median absolute deviation from the median, multiplied by a scaling factor so that it is equivalent to the sd for the case of the normal distribution).  These have the advantage that they always exist (so will work, for example, with the Cauchy distribution), also I think they're closer to what users should really want in most applications.  Similarly, we'd replace se_mean by mad_se which is just mad_sd/sqrt(n_eff). Then for the quantiles, now we report 2.5%, 25%, 50%, 75%, 97.5%.  OK, we don't need 50% anymore.  I'd recommend removing 2.5% and 97.5% too (or maybe not, I'm not quite sure; on one hand, focusing on these intervals is bad practice, and these tail values have lots of simulation noise; on the other, it can be good for people to see some wide uncertainty bounds).
> >
> > So here's the new output:
> >
> > median mad_sd 25% 75% n_eff mad_se Rhat
> >
> > You can see that I changed the order a bit.  I find se_mean (or, equivalently, mad_se) a bit difficult to explain.  I end up just saying it's sd/sqrt(n_eff) (or mad_sd/sqrt(n_eff), but, if so, it makes sense for it to appear _after_ n_eff in the table.  Finally, I kept Rhat at the end because it's convenient to scan the output and look at R_hat.
>

> Exception thrown at line 202: integrate_ode_bdf: parameter vector[1] is 1.#INF, but must be finite!

Under Windows, IEEE infinity values are printed as "1.#INF". That means that the first value in your parameters is infinity and the integrate_ode_bdf() call from Stan stopped before it tried to call the CVode BDF integrator.

I'm sure the parameters are being pushed into a space where the CVodr integrator fails in a similar way.

Jonathon O'Brien

messages.body_plain:
Have you tried running a small simulated data set on
a single chain?  Stan shouldn't be crashing the system no
matter what happens.  But if a single iteration takes
1000 leapfrog steps, it can get hung up in one iteration
and that's the granularity we current check for interrupts.
You can try setting the max tree depth lower to see if that
still crashes---if not, you may just be crushing the memory
of the system you're on.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
> On Feb 22, 2017, at 3:42 AM, Ewan Keith <ewan.k...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Thanks. Would this method of assignment have worked in a previous version? The thread linked to in my original post and Ben's response seem to suggest so.

No.  The Stan language has been fully backward compatible since
version 1.0 with a single exception---you can't access lp__ directly
any more.

The behavior with matrices is confusing for a lot of people, but
it's the same as the behavior in R.

> What I'm trying to achieve is a matrix with common priors on all entries, but with a a subset of entries fixed at pre-specified values. For example:
>
> [X, 0, 0,
>  X, 0, 0,
>  0, X, 0,
>  0, X, 0,
>  0, 0, X]
>
> Where '0' entries are fixed at zero, and 'X' entries have prior N(0, 1). I suspect this could be achieved by simply specifying all matrix entries individually in the model, but was looking to see if there was a less verbose solution (in this case by using a vector of position indices).

Maybe you could do this in a less verbose way, but it wouldn't be
as clear.  Given that it's not a submatrix, matrix slicing won't work.
You'd have to do something like this:

data {
  int[5] is;

parameters {
  vector[5] x_raw;

model {
  vector[15] x_vec = rep_vector(0, 15);
  matrix[5, 3] x;
  x_vec[x_non_zero] = x_raw;
  x = to_matrix(x_vec);

...

You could also define x as a transformed parameter, just make x_vec
a local variable inside { } because you don't want to save that.
And be careful of the order in to_matrix (I can't recall which order
we use).

- Bob

>            for(i in 1:N){
>
>  		for(l in 1:47){

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Further strategies to deal with divergent transitions
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Further strategies to deal with divergent transitions
messages.body_plain:
First of all, you don't need these epsilon lower bounds:

  real<lower=0.00000001> nu;

If your estimates for nu are getting that close to zero, there's
a problem with your model.  In that case, we recommend priors rather
than these hard constraints.

In general, constraining parameters can make the fitting much much
harder if the unconstrained parameter would sample beyond the
constraint boundary.  What happens is that on the unconstrained scale
is that Stan has to explore out to plus or minus infinity to get
some draws.  And it biases the outcome.

I don't understand your model, but those exp(normal_lpdf(...)) can
be bad news due to underflow.  I'd suggest keeping everything on
the log scale.

Is that likelihood a mixture model?  Otherwise, I don't understand
why you're using log_sum_exp over T rather than sum.

Ther'es a lot of thing syou can vectorize as well, but that's just
an efficiency issue.

- Bob

messages.subject: Estimating random slopes with missing data and comparing within/between-subject designs
messages.subject_clean: Estimating random slopes with missing data and comparing within/between-subject designs
messages.body_plain:
I am analyzing a data set for someone in which participants make two binary decisions (related to art preference) in either one or two conditions each. Individual participants were tested across 6 experiments split between these designs. This results in some participants with 1 response in Condition A and 1 response in Condition B (within-subjects design), some participants with 2 responses in Condition A and some participants with 2 responses in Condition B (between-subjects design). In addition to assuming that participants will vary in their overall propensity to make one decision or the other (random intercept) it also seems reasonable to consider the possibility that they would vary in their response to the experimental manipulation (random slope). A similar argument might be made for variation in response at the level of the experiments as well. Therefore, the appropriate formula seems to be:

stan_glmer(decision ~ condition + (condition | participant_id) + (condition | experiment_id), data = data_frame, family = binomial, adapt_delta=.999)

This fits the model just fine, and the results look reasonable. However, it is interesting that this model *does* work so well. Trying variations of this model using glmer results in an error concerning identifiability, presumably because the model is trying to estimate random slopes for some participants that have no responses in one of the two conditions. I believe that rstanarm deals with those cases by imputing slopes based on the joint posterior: This means (roughly) that the random slopes for participants in the between-subject experiments will be based on the random slopes for participants in the within-subject experiments. This seems fine, and the specific random slopes for the between-subject experiments are not important. My question is whether this understanding is correct or whether I am missing some pernicious element of modelling the data in this manner. Further, we would ultimately like to compare performance across experimental design, for example using:

stan_glmer(decision ~ condition * design + (condition | participant_id) + (condition | experiment_id), data = data_frame, family = binomial, adapt_delta=.999)

Here, design refers to whether a given experiment employed a within- or between-subjects design. Again, the model fits and everything appears to be in order, but I am a little cautious in part due to earlier critiques of within/between-subject comparisons of this nature using more “traditional” techniques (for example, Erlebacher, 1977). I believe this sort of comparison to be a non-issue with stan_glmer, but I wanted a second opinion before committing.

Thanks in advance!

messages.body_plain:
Stan doesn't support discrete parameters.  So you won't be able
to write your own discrete sampler.  Or if you think you do, you'll
find it won't work in inference because the step functions involved
break derivatives.

You will be able to marginalize out, though.

You might write a simple normal mixture model in JAGS model like this:

  z[n] ~ dbern(theta);
  y[n] ~ dnorm(mu[z[n]], sigma[z[n]]);

In Stan, you need to marginalize out that z parameter.  So you
write the same thing with no discrete parameters as:

  target += log_sum_exp(log(theta) + normal_lpdf(y[n] | mu[1], sigma[1]),
                        log1m(theta) + normal_lpdf(y[n] | mu[2], sigma[2]));

Works the same way with more than two values for z.

It gives you the exact same inference on the parameters mu and sigma,
except it's a lot faster and a lot more robust (as in it can be more
than two orders of magnitude faster).  No surprise---just a consequence
of the Rao-Blackwell theorem and the fact that discrete sampling tends to
be intractable in practice---it just mixes terribly if there are any
correlations and has a really hard time with tails.

You can reconstruct anything you need to do with z.
You can see this implicitly in the mixture formulation above, where
mu[1], sigma[1] and mu[2], sigma[2] are both used.

You can reconstruct everything you need in expectation.  Specifically,
you can calculate Pr[z[n] == 1 | y]

Check out the manual chapter on latent discrete parameters to see how all
that works.

Or you could do the same marginalization in JAGS using the zeros trick.
Others have found this hugely sped up their state-space models with latent
discrete parameters.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Difficulties using categorical() distribution
messages.body_plain:
The parameter for this NHPP's model is a discrete stochastic process, the gamma process, that for this case is also the mean-value function for the NHPP.  I don't see how the marginalizing approach would work for this application.
I do believe that it would be trivial to code a user-defined function for an inverse transform sampler that generates discrete values from the gamma process.  All that would need to be called from this custom function would be functions to query from a gamma variable's cdf and to generate random uniform numbers.  It would also necessitate performing the call to this custom function outside the bounds of the time steps in the main Stan model's sampling progression.  However, I have no idea on the level of work involved with making this capability available in Stan.

REub

On Wed, Feb 22, 2017 at 4:37 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:

> Stan doesn't support discrete parameters.  So you won't be able
> to write your own discrete sampler.  Or if you think you do, you'll
> find it won't work in inference because the step functions involved
> break derivatives.
>
> You will be able to marginalize out, though.
>
> You might write a simple normal mixture model in JAGS model like this:
>
>   z[n] ~ dbern(theta);
>   y[n] ~ dnorm(mu[z[n]], sigma[z[n]]);
>
> In Stan, you need to marginalize out that z parameter.  So you
> write the same thing with no discrete parameters as:
>
>   target += log_sum_exp(log(theta) + normal_lpdf(y[n] | mu[1], sigma[1]),
>                         log1m(theta) + normal_lpdf(y[n] | mu[2], sigma[2]));
>
> Works the same way with more than two values for z.
>
> It gives you the exact same inference on the parameters mu and sigma,
> except it's a lot faster and a lot more robust (as in it can be more
> than two orders of magnitude faster).  No surprise---just a consequence
> of the Rao-Blackwell theorem and the fact that discrete sampling tends to
> be intractable in practice---it just mixes terribly if there are any
> correlations and has a really hard time with tails.
>
> You can reconstruct anything you need to do with z.
> You can see this implicitly in the mixture formulation above, where
> mu[1], sigma[1] and mu[2], sigma[2] are both used.
>
> You can reconstruct everything you need in expectation.  Specifically,
> you can calculate Pr[z[n] == 1 | y]
>
> Check out the manual chapter on latent discrete parameters to see how all
> that works.
>
> Or you could do the same marginalization in JAGS using the zeros trick.
> Others have found this hugely sped up their state-space models with latent
> discrete parameters.
>
> - Bob

> > > > ##########################
> > > > Model (JAGS)
> > > > ##########################
> > > > #Description: Doubly stochastic NHPP, with a Gamma process for the cumulative intensity function (Kuo-Ghosh model).
> > > > #Note, Theta(t) must be constructed from the individual r intervals.  Otherwise, the resulting random variables for
> > > > #Theta(t) fail to meet the non-decreasing requirement.
> > > >
> > > > #unlike OpenBUGS, JAGS forbids stochastic nodes to be declared twice
> > > > data {
> > > > ##INDICES,START##
> > > >  #JAGS appears to not support expressions for indices in the model, create a variable for this index maximum
> > > >  T1 <- length(N)
> > > >  T2 <- dim(pr_r)
> > > > ##INDICES,STOP##
> > > > ##LIKELIHOODDATA,START##
> > > >  for (i in 2:length(N)) {
> > > >   #zero the dummy variables for the custom sampling distribution
> > > >   dummylogN[i-1] <- 0
> > > >  }
> > > > ##LIKELIHOODDATA,STOP##
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > model {
> > > >  #terms for simplifying the joint loglikelihood below (these are not dependent on independent variables and are located outside the area preprocessed)

> > > >  for (i in 2:T1) {
> > > >   #terms for simplifying the joint loglikelihood below
> > > >   A[i-1] <- Theta[i]-Theta[i-1]
> > > >  }
> > > > ##LIKELIHOOD,START##
> > > >  #joint likelihood function
> > > >  for (i in 2:T1) {
> > > >   #terms for simplifying the joint loglikelihood below
> > > >   BN[i-1] <- N[i]-N[i-1]
> > > >   #Using the zeros trick for custom loglikelihood
> > > >   dummylogN[i-1] ~ dpois(logN[i-1])
> > > >   logN[i-1] <- -loglikelihoodN[i-1] + C
> > > >   loglikelihoodN[i-1] <- phi*(-1*logfact(BN[i-1])+BN[i-1]*log(A[i-1])-A[i-1])
> > > >  }
> > > > ##LIKELIHOOD,STOP##
> > > >
> > > > ##VARIABLE,1##
> > > >  #prior distribution for Theta (gamma process)
> > > >  #translation of the stochastic node intervals to cumulative form
> > > >  Theta[1] <- 0
> > > >  for (i in 2:T1) {
> > > >   Theta[i] <- Theta[i-1]+r[i-1]
> > > >   #Using the dcat distribution to generate values from the gamma prior's PMF
> > > >   #pr_r[interval,PMF] matrix contains an array of point estimates for each interval's PMF
> > > >   #Nindices[] array of possible values for N(t)=n
> > > >   r_[i-1] ~ dcat(pr_r[i-1,])#sample the dcat rv to get the index
> > > >   r[i-1] <- Nindices[r_[i-1]]#transform the index to the interval count
> > > >  }
> > > > }

> > > > #FN1: "A Poisson(phi) observation of zero has likelihood exp(-phi), so if our observed data is a set of 0's, and

> > > > #be > 0 as it is a Poisson mean, and so we may need to add a suitable constant to ensure that it is positive.)"
