messages.body_plain:
> On Feb 22, 2017, at 7:22 PM, Reuben Johnston <reuben.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> The parameter for this NHPP's model is a discrete stochastic process, the gamma process, that for this case is also the mean-value function for the NHPP.  I don't see how the marginalizing approach would work for this application.

Does the gamma process have correlated outputs at each time
state like a Gaussian process or are the outputs conditionally
independent based on the discrete states like an HMM?

If it's the latter, it'd work like the forward algorithm in HMMs.
If it's the former, you're probably out of luck because the
margninalization will be intractable.

I had a hard time seeing the overall structure of the process from
your code.  But then I didn't understand the Wikipedia page on
Gamma processes either.

> I do believe that it would be trivial to code a user-defined function for an inverse transform sampler that generates discrete values from the gamma process.  All that would need to be called from this custom function would be functions to query from a gamma variable's cdf and to generate random uniform numbers.  It would also necessitate performing the call to this custom function outside the bounds of the time steps in the main Stan model's sampling progression.  However, I have no idea on the level of work involved with making this capability available in Stan.

You could code that, but you can't call random number generators in
Stan's model block---only after the fact in generated quantities.  The
reason we do this is because they don't play nicely with inference.
They basically perform something like the "cut" in BUGS implicitly.
We lose the information connection statistically and we lose the
derivative information computationally.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
Artificial hard upper bounds are almost always a bad idea.
If you guess wrong and there's any measurable mass above
the bound, you essentially get both biased estimates and
a computational problem as you try to run off to infinity
on the unconstrained scale.  But if the data's normal,
that's exactly what your estimate of nu is going to try to do.

Someone else probably knows how much data we need to estimate
nu, but you may want to do some experiments yourself by
simulating from a student t with various nu and seeing what
you get for estimates.

I'm also not sure what it means to have nu < 1.  It seems
like the Cauchy is a reasonable lower-bound on fatness of
tails.  Please let me know if that's not right!  In Stan,
that constraint would be:

parameters {
  real<lower = 1> nu;

But then it might also make sense to put a prior
on 1 / nu and transform (even a uniform) and transform:

parameters {
  real<lower = 0, upper = 1> inv_nu;
  ...

transformed parameters {
  real<lower = 1> nu = inv(inv_nu);
  ...

I never got a proper stats education, so I have to work out what we
get from first principles with the Jacobian adjustment to the transformed
uniform:

If

  X ~ uniform(0, 1);

and

  Y = 1 / X

then

  Y in (1, infinity)

and

  p_Y(y) = |d/dy 1/y| uniform(1/y | 0, 1)

         = 1 / y^2

Now that looks familiar.

  https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pareto_distribution

It's just Pareto(1, 1).   And the Wikipedia neatly summarizes that
if Y ~ Pareto(1, 1), then

  Pr[Y > y] = 1 / y

In Stan you can code the Pareto up directly:

parameters {
  real<lower = 1> nu;

model {
  nu ~ pareto(1, 1);

No idea if that's a good idea, but it let me do some math
exercises on our mailing list.  Hope I didn't botch something.

- Bob

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Difficulties using categorical() distribution
messages.body_plain:
I am using the counting process, non-stationary form of the Gamma process and I think of it as being very similar to the non-homogeneous Poisson process, but the interarrival times are gamma distributed, rather than exponential (as in the NHPP).  A more formal definition is provided by van Noortwijk:

"Let v(t) be a non-decreasing, right-continuous,real-valued function for t>=0, with v(0)=0. The gamma process with shape function v(t)>0 and scale parameter u>0 is a continuous-time stochastic process {X(t),t>=0} with the following properties:
(1) X(0)=0 with probability one;
(2) X(tau)-X(t)~Ga(v(tau)-v(t),u), for all tau>t>=0;
(3) X(t) has independent increments

Pages 8-10 of 2007, Merrick and Soyer provide the best description of how I am using the gamma process.  It will also be described in my dissertation, but that is not finished yet.  A very concise description is as follows.

I estimated the values for the Gamma process's probability mass function and passed in the results for a subset of the realizations (e.g., pr(Θ(t)=n, for n=1:250) as an array to BUGS/JAGS.  I then used the dcat() distribution with this pmf, to simulate values from the Gamma process prior (i.e., dcat provides samples from Θ(t) in the range 1<=N<=250, according to the probabilities in the pmf passed to dcat), in the sampling steps in BUGS/JAGS.  In this model, the parameter Θ(t) is used as the cumulative intensity (or mean-value) function for a non-homogeneous Poisson process.  For this alternative, the prior for Θ(t)~GammaProcess(c*Λ(t),c), where the hyper-parameter Λ(t) is described as a best guess for the NHPP mean value function and c is a constant describing the measure of certainty for the best guess given the prior history, where lower values indicate higher confidence in the best guess.  I am using the counting form of the NHPP, so my data are grouped-interval counts over time.  An example dataset for the intervals t=(0-10], (10-20], (20-30], would be the respective cumulative counts 10, 25, and 50.

References:
* 2008, Merrick, Soyer, Computational Issues in Semiparametric Bayesian Replacement Models, Technical Report TR-2008-4
* 2007, Merrick, Soyer, Semiparametric Bayesian Decision Models for Optimal Replacement, Technical Report TR-2007-4
* 2007, van Noortwijk, A survey of the application of gamma processes in maintenance

It would also necessitate performing the call to this custom function outside the bounds of the time steps in the main Stan model's sampling progression.  However, I have no idea on the level of work involved with making this capability available in Stan.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] questions around hierarchical ordered logit
messages.body_plain:
We don't have good prior recommendations for these as far as I know.  I think global cut points are more common than varying ones, but we're big fans of hierarchical modeling, so if you can figure it out, that'd be great.  I didn't see any hierarchical structure in your model or a prior for c_vote.

Empty loops won't do anything---the C++ compiler is usually good enough to ignore all this.

For standard errors on the posterior means, we divide the posterior standard deviation by the sqrt of the number of effective samples.  It's all estimated.

- Bob

Thanks to you both, and sorry for not remembering to look at the prior recommendations wiki page in the first place!

On Thu, Feb 23, 2017 at 5:22 PM Aki Vehtari <aki.v...@aalto.fi> wrote:

> See our "Prior Choice Recommendations" wiki page and search for Prior for degrees of freedom in Student's t distribution, which says
> A recommended easy default option is
> nu ~ gamma(2,0.1);
> This was proposed and anlysed by Juárez and Steel (2010) (Model-based clustering of non-Gaussian panel data based on skew-t distributions. Journal of Business & Economic Statistics 28, 52–66.). Juárez and Steel compare this to Jeffreys prior and report that the difference is small. Simpson et al (2014) (arXiv:1403.4630) propose a theoretically well justified "penalised complexity (PC) prior", which they show to have a good behavior for the degrees of freedom, too. PC prior might be the best choice, but requires numerical computation of the prior (which could computed in a grid and interpolated etc.). It is available as INLA:::inla.pc.ddof for dof>2 and a standardized Student's-t. It would be feasible to implement it in Stan, but it would require some work. Unfortunately no-one has compared PC prior and this gamma prior directly, but based on the discussion with Daniel Simpson, although PC prior would be better this gamma(2,0.1) prior is not a bad choice. Thus, I would use it until someone implements the PC prior for degrees of freedom of the Student's t in Stan.
>
> Like Bob, I also recommend adding a lower limit with a constraint in the parameter declaration (and add this to wiki, too)
>
> It's possible that Pareto with some parameters could be close to the gamma(2,0.1) recommended above
>
> Aki
>
>

> >   }

> >     y ~ student_t( nu , mu , sigma ) ;
> >     mu ~ normal( 0 , 1 ) ;
> >     sigma ~ weibull( 2 , 1 ) ;
> >     nu ~ ?;
> >   }
> >
> > What might be a reasonable prior on nu?
> >
> > One thought is that values for nu greater than about 30 really don't differentiate from each other in terms of the resulting form of the student-t, so should I put a hard upper bound at 30?
> >
> > And should the lower bound be 0, or 1? I know that nu=1 is the cauchy, but I don't know that values of nu less than one even make sense.
> >
> > Thanks in advance for your thoughts.
> >

messages.body_plain:
I was reading chapter '14.2 Change Point Models' of the Stan manual, specifically the example and model related to the coal mining disasters.

Could the conditional operator be replaced by a continuous step mixing function in order to simplify the model?
I mean  replacing:

 Dt ~ Poisson(t < s ? e : l)

With something like:

  alpha = 1.0 / (1 + exp(s - t - 0.5)^15);                     // step function modeling rate change
  Dt ~ Poisson( e*(1-alpha) + l*alpha );

We can see that at the change point alpha is :

1.0 / (1 + exp(0 - 0.5)^15) = 0.9994472

and

1.0 / (1 + exp(1 - 0.5)^15) =  0.0005527786

I have implemented the example in full and the results are consistent with all the other solutions I have seen. Full code below.

Is this a valid way of modelling this problem in Stan?

Thanks,
Antonio

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
# coal mining disasters change point test

require(Rcpp)
require(rstan)

stanmodel <- '

data {
  // signal data
  int<lower=1>          N;
  int                       y[N];          // value
}

parameters {

  real<lower=1>             event;       // change point day
  real<lower=0>             lambda[2]; // rates before and after change point
}

model {

  event  ~ uniform(1,112); // [1, max(day)]
  lambda ~ uniform(0,10);  // [1, max(y)]

  for (i in 1:N)
  {
    real alpha;
    real beta;

    alpha = 1.0 / (1 + exp(event - i - 0.5)^15);                     // step function modeling change point
    beta  = lambda[1] *(1-alpha) +  lambda[2]*alpha;          // rates mixing
    y[i] ~ poisson(beta);

  }
}
'

abline(v=mean(t), col='red')
plot(y, cex=0.8, xlab='year', ylab='d')
lines(y)

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When can a sample become infinite?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] When can a sample become infinite?
messages.body_plain:
The problem is that double-precision floating point isn't very
precise.  For example, if you have

  real x;

  real y = exp(x);

then if x > 400, y will be infinite.

So when gradients are infinite, it's usually an issue with
overflow.  Or underflow and then a log if it's negative.

When you say infinite moments, you mean the posterior mean
as you get from printing?

There's a discussion in the manual of problematic posteriors,
and you can see that some kinds of additive non-identifiability
lead to improper posteriors---they have a ridge of constant
density running out to infinity.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Vectorization and non-centered parameterization with nested groups
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Vectorization and non-centered parameterization with nested groups
messages.body_plain:
You want to use the non-centered parameterizations when you
don't have much data and the centered parameterizations when
you do.  You want to get rid of the funnel and tiled ellipses
in the posterior in favor of things that look a unit
circle (that happens when the parameters aren't correlated
in the posterior and have unit scales).

For vectorization, you can replace this:

    vector[S] state_effect;
    vector[C] county_mu;
    vector[C] county_effect;

    state_effect = sigma_state * state_raw;

    for (c in 1:C)
        county_mu[c] = beta_funding * funding[c] + state_effect[state[c]];

    county_effect = county_mu + sigma_county * county_raw;

with

  vector[C] county_effect = beta_funding * funding
                          + sigma_state * state_raw[state]
                          + sigma_count * count_raw;

And then you can just drop it into the regression along with beta0
unless you want to save it in the output.  I find expanding things
all the way out like this is helpful because you can see the predictors
and the scales all in one place.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: Estimating random slopes with missing data and comparing within/between-subject designs
messages.subject_clean: Estimating random slopes with missing data and comparing within/between-subject designs
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jon,

I wouldn't say that rstanarm is "imputing slopes based on the joint posterior", although I think I know what you mean. It's not really imputation but more borrowing information. But yes I think you have the basic idea correct.

Regarding non-identifiability, the priors (even the defaults) that stan_glmer uses should in general help make it more robust to non-identifiability than regular glmer. There can still be problems, but priors help a lot. Also, how many levels (unique values) does participant_id have?

I'm not familiar with Erlebacher (1977), so I can't really say if the concerns in that paper are or are not an issue here. Can you give a brief summary?

Jonah

On Wednesday, February 22, 2017 at 1:56:59 PM UTC-5, Jon Fawcett wrote:
>
> I am analyzing a data set for someone in which participants make two binary decisions (related to art preference) in either one or two conditions each. Individual participants were tested across 6 experiments split between these designs. This results in some participants with 1 response in Condition A and 1 response in Condition B (within-subjects design), some participants with 2 responses in Condition A and some participants with 2 responses in Condition B (between-subjects design). In addition to assuming that participants will vary in their overall propensity to make one decision or the other (random intercept) it also seems reasonable to consider the possibility that they would vary in their response to the experimental manipulation (random slope). A similar argument might be made for variation in response at the level of the experiments as well. Therefore, the appropriate formula seems to be:
>
>
> stan_glmer(decision ~ condition + (condition | participant_id) + (condition | experiment_id), data = data_frame, family = binomial, adapt_delta=.999)
>
>
> This fits the model just fine, and the results look reasonable. However, it is interesting that this model *does* work so well. Trying variations of this model using glmer results in an error concerning identifiability, presumably because the model is trying to estimate random slopes for some participants that have no responses in one of the two conditions. I believe that rstanarm deals with those cases by imputing slopes based on the joint posterior: This means (roughly) that the random slopes for participants in the between-subject experiments will be based on the random slopes for participants in the within-subject experiments. This seems fine, and the specific random slopes for the between-subject experiments are not important. My question is whether this understanding is correct or whether I am missing some pernicious element of modelling the data in this manner. Further, we would ultimately like to compare performance across experimental design, for example using:
>
>
> stan_glmer(decision ~ condition * design + (condition | participant_id) + (condition | experiment_id), data = data_frame, family = binomial, adapt_delta=.999)
>
>
> Here, design refers to whether a given experiment employed a within- or between-subjects design. Again, the model fits and everything appears to be in order, but I am a little cautious in part due to earlier critiques of within/between-subject comparisons of this nature using more “traditional” techniques (for example, Erlebacher, 1977). I believe this sort of comparison to be a non-issue with stan_glmer, but I wanted a second opinion before committing.
>
>
> Thanks in advance!

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Difficulties using categorical() distribution
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Difficulties using categorical() distribution
messages.body_plain:
I fear nobody's going to see this who will be able to
answer it.  Would you mind reposting the question with
"gamma process" in the title and hopefully some of
our devs or users who know more about these processes than
me can help out.

If there are unknown count variables, they usually can't
be marginalized out.  If there are just categorical
variables that are data-item related, they usually can
be marginalized out.

- Bob

> On Feb 23, 2017, at 8:27 AM, Reuben Johnston <reuben.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> I am using the counting process, non-stationary form of the Gamma process and I think of it as being very similar to the non-homogeneous Poisson process, but the interarrival times are gamma distributed, rather than exponential (as in the NHPP).  A more formal definition is provided by van Noortwijk:
>
> "Let v(t) be a non-decreasing, right-continuous,real-valued function for t>=0, with v(0)=0. The gamma process with shape function v(t)>0 and scale parameter u>0 is a continuous-time stochastic process {X(t),t>=0} with the following properties:
> (1) X(0)=0 with probability one;
> (2) X(tau)-X(t)~Ga(v(tau)-v(t),u), for all tau>t>=0;
> (3) X(t) has independent increments
>
> Pages 8-10 of 2007, Merrick and Soyer provide the best description of how I am using the gamma process.  It will also be described in my dissertation, but that is not finished yet.  A very concise description is as follows.
>
> I estimated the values for the Gamma process's probability mass function and passed in the results for a subset of the realizations (e.g., pr(Θ(t)=n, for n=1:250) as an array to BUGS/JAGS.  I then used the dcat() distribution with this pmf, to simulate values from the Gamma process prior (i.e., dcat provides samples from Θ(t) in the range 1<=N<=250, according to the probabilities in the pmf passed to dcat), in the sampling steps in BUGS/JAGS.  In this model, the parameter Θ(t) is used as the cumulative intensity (or mean-value) function for a non-homogeneous Poisson process.  For this alternative, the prior for Θ(t)~GammaProcess(c*Λ(t),c), where the hyper-parameter Λ(t) is described as a best guess for the NHPP mean value function and c is a constant describing the measure of certainty for the best guess given the prior history, where lower values indicate higher confidence in the best guess.  I am using the counting form of the NHPP, so my data are grouped-interval counts over time.  An example dataset for the intervals t=(0-10], (10-20], (20-30], would be the respective cumulative counts 10, 25, and 50.
>
> References:
> * 2008, Merrick, Soyer, Computational Issues in Semiparametric Bayesian Replacement Models, Technical Report TR-2008-4
> * 2007, Merrick, Soyer, Semiparametric Bayesian Decision Models for Optimal Replacement, Technical Report TR-2007-4
> * 2007, van Noortwijk, A survey of the application of gamma processes in maintenance
>
>
> On Wed, Feb 22, 2017 at 10:36 PM, Bob Carpenter <ca...@alias-i.com> wrote:
>
> > On Feb 22, 2017, at 7:22 PM, Reuben Johnston <reuben.a...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > The parameter for this NHPP's model is a discrete stochastic process, the gamma process, that for this case is also the mean-value function for the NHPP.  I don't see how the marginalizing approach would work for this application.
>
> Does the gamma process have correlated outputs at each time
> state like a Gaussian process or are the outputs conditionally
> independent based on the discrete states like an HMM?
>
> If it's the latter, it'd work like the forward algorithm in HMMs.
> If it's the former, you're probably out of luck because the
> margninalization will be intractable.
>
> I had a hard time seeing the overall structure of the process from
> your code.  But then I didn't understand the Wikipedia page on
> Gamma processes either.
>
> > I do believe that it would be trivial to code a user-defined function for an inverse transform sampler that generates discrete values from the gamma process.  All that would need to be called from this custom function would be functions to query from a gamma variable's cdf and to generate random uniform numbers.  It would also necessitate performing the call to this custom function outside the bounds of the time steps in the main Stan model's sampling progression.  However, I have no idea on the level of work involved with making this capability available in Stan.
>
> You could code that, but you can't call random number generators in
> Stan's model block---only after the fact in generated quantities.  The
> reason we do this is because they don't play nicely with inference.
> They basically perform something like the "cut" in BUGS implicitly.
> We lose the information connection statistically and we lose the
> derivative information computationally.
>
> - Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] How does stan computation time scale with number of iterations?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] How does stan computation time scale with number of iterations?
messages.body_plain:
The time difference comes from the different adaptation
achieved in the two settings.  I’m assuming that you’re
using RStan (note that Stan is not capitalized) in which
case half of the transitions are left for adaptation and
half for sampling.  When you run 100 total transitions
you have only 50 warmup transitions which is almost
always insufficient to adequate tune the sampler
parameters.  Problems arising with more adaptation
indicate a problematic model.

Additionally, if you are running multiple chains you
should be more sensitive to other problems that can
cause different adaptations.

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] New paper using Stan to test for discrimination
messages.body_plain:
Yes, it's the distribution of p(Y|X) where X is drawn from a two-component normal mixture with Y denoting component membership. p(Y|X) is of course simple to compute but we weren't sure anyone had ever used its distribution like this before (in particular, to approximate a beta or logit-normal for computational speedups).

On Friday, February 24, 2017 at 5:47:24 PM UTC-8, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> Thanks for sharing.  I think your discriminant distribution
> is the component membership probability in a two-component
> normal mixture model.  Am I understanding that properly?
>
> I love that people are using Stan for this kind of work.  It's
> exactly what we hoped people would do.
>
> - Bob
>
>
> > On Feb 24, 2017, at 5:49 PM, Emma Pierson <2plus...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > We recently used Stan to fit a statistical model which tests for discrimination. We describe the work in this paper: https://5harad.com/papers/fast-threshold-test.pdf. We found that we were able to accelerate inference by several orders of magnitude by using a class of distributions that we are calling discriminant distributions. We would welcome any feedback on the distribution, the model, or the paper in general!

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, Jonah!
You are correct, this is precisely what I meant (albeit expressed in an imprecise manner, it would seem). As for the number of levels, I have somewhere in the order of ~600 participants and 6 experiments. But again, for approximately half of those participants there is 1 observation for each condition and for the remaining half are 2 observations in one of the the two conditions (meaning that those participants lack entirely data in the remaining condition).

As for Erlebacher (1977), the precise concerns voiced in that article are not relevant because he is talking about trying to compare designs using Frequentist ANOVAs. However, the thesis is that psychologists of that era had been drawing comparisons across within- and between-subject studies for some time in a misleading or wasteful manner. Erlebacher proposed to correct this by providing a variation of a standard ANOVA capable of making across design comparisons. I really just want to ensure that I am not analogously blind to an error in the current model. In short, if by running the aforementioned model:

stan_glmer(decision ~ condition * design + (condition | participant_id) + (condition | experiment_id), data = data_frame, family = binomial, adapt_delta=.999)

I am able to conclude that the effect of condition is (for example) larger for studies in which this variable is manipulated within-subjects relative to between-subjects (the condition x design interaction), I am all set!

messages.subject: Sampling not done because 'y is not positive definite'
messages.subject_clean: Sampling not done because 'y is not positive definite'
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm fitting a non-linear mixed effects model with 25 random effects and 5 group-level predictors. 12 of these random effects are interactions, so x and z are random effects as well as the interaction xz. I do not specify any priors myself since I have no knowledge about the probability distributions of the various variables.
I have a data set of 4000 observations (200 groups with 20 observations per group). All continuous predictor variables were mean centred. The reciprocal transformation of the response variable (multiplied by large constant) was taken to ameliorate heteroscedasticity in the model.

When fitting the model using the R package 'brms' (which relies on rstan) I get the following error:

> SAMPLING FOR MODEL 'gaussian(identity) brms-model' NOW (CHAIN 1).
> [1] "Error in sampler$call_sampler(args_list[[i]]) : "
> [2] "  model14a86bff6439_file14a877266e59_namespace::write_array: y is not positive definite."
> [1] "error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done"

When using 'rstanarm' (with QR=FALSE and QR=TRUE) I get the following error

> fixed-effect model matrix is rank deficient so dropping 128 columns / coefficients

Both errors suggests possible collinearity issues, while the latter error suggests the presence of collinearity in my fixed effects design matrix, meaning some columns can be expressed as linear combinations of other columns. However, trying to identify these colums with the function findLinearCombos(Fixed Effects Matrix) (package caret) did not show any linear dependencies. Executing the same function on the random effects design matrix Zt did show many linear dependencies and suggests me to remove, for example, "b[Greedy problem:1]"  and "b[Regret2 problem:1]" from the model.

When I remove 3 random effects, sampling begins, but the model does not converge, with Rhats > 1.1. Doubling the number of observations (200 groups with 40 observations per group) does not help either. I have tried fitting a model that considers the interactions effects as fixed effects instead of random effects and this works fine, so the issue lies with considering these interactions as random effects.

My question: Is it simply impossible given the data set I use to find a stable fit for a model that considers (this many) 2-way interactions as random effects? Is there anything else I could try to resolve the 'not positive definite' issue that prevents sampling to start.

p.s. I also tried to fit the fit model using rstan directly. However, the stancode provided by the brm-model gave the following error in rstan
> Error in basename(fname) : path too long
> In addition: Warning message:
> In normalizePath(path.expand(path), winslash, mustWork) :
>   path[1]="// generated with brms 1.5.0
> functions {
> }
> ...
>  vector[N] Z_1_25;
>   int<lower=1> NC_1;
>   int prior_only;  // should the likeliho [... truncated]

Is there a maximum code length for rstan?

I went through the examples in Stan’s guideline but most of them are talking about Bayesian inference and fitting data to the models.

I need to work on those samples for estimating small failure probabilities.

I would appreciate it if you could guide me in this regard.

Thank you,

messages.body_plain:
There are R and MATLAB interfaces to Stan (see mc-stan.org <http://mc-stan.org> under Interfaces
tab).

There's no requirement that the density from which Stan samples
be a Bayesian posterior.  You can write down any old density you
want and Stan will sample from it.  It's just that we usually condition
on data as well as constants, giving us a Bayesian posterior.

If you said more about the density you want to sample from, we could
say more.

- Bob

messages.body_plain:
OK, then a few more questions and comments.

1.  Do you want just a center and just a scale as options, or
if they show up, would both be required?

2.  Can they occur with lower and upper bounds?  If so, the center
and scale seem to make most sense on the unconstrained scale.  Right
now, we have sigma_unc in (-inf, inf), and it transforms for <lower=0>
to

  sigma = exp(sigma_conc)

So that if we have

  real<lower=0, center=20, scale=5> sigma;

it would produce the transformed type:

  sigma = exp(5 * sigma_unc + 20)

3.  We would probably want to allow parameters as values of
center and scale.  Then we start getting Jacobians we need
to worry about because they may be constant in the transformed
parameter, but not in other parameters used to define bounds.

4.  What types other than real should these work for?  I'm thinking
the ones that are unbounded make most sense: ordered, pos_ordered, cov_matrix
(and of course, vector, row_vector, and matrix).

- Bob

I also realized we did say something on our priors page.  I should look
at our own Wiki:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations

• Prior for cutpoints in ordered logit or probit regression
  • For full Bayes, uniform priors typically should be ok, I think.
  • For modal estimation, put in some pseudodata in each category to prevent "cutpoint collapse."
  • Cutpoints are ordered (by definition). Put the prior on the differences between the cutpoints rather than the cutpoints themselves.
  • Alternatively, put a prior on the cutpoints and partially pool them, not to a constant, but to a linear function. That is, if the cutpoints are c[1],...,c[K], don't do c[k] ~ normal(mu, sigma); instead do c[k] ~ normal(a + b*k, sigma), estimating the hyperparameters a and b from data. It will probably make sense to put informative priors on a, b, and sigma too.

messages.body_plain:
> On Feb 26, 2017, at 6:36 PM, Michael Betancourt <betan...@gmail.com> wrote:
>

> >
> > 3.  We would probably want to allow parameters as values of
> > center and scale.  Then we start getting Jacobians we need
> > to worry about because they may be constant in the transformed
> > parameter, but not in other parameters used to define bounds.
>
> Do we though?  If we’re thinking about this purely as a means
> of standardizing parameters then why not limit the locations and
> scales to data?

I was thinking of only allowing these locations and scales to be data.  Allowing them to be parameters is interesting but it's an idea I haven't fully thought through.  Only allowing as data would solve most of our use cases, I think.

> > 4.  What types other than real should these work for?  I'm thinking
> > the ones that are unbounded make most sense: ordered, pos_ordered, cov_matrix
> > (and of course, vector, row_vector, and matrix).
>
> We can avoid the potential confusion between constrained and
> unconstrained scales entirely by limiting <center=, scale=> to
> unconstrained scalar parameters.

It would be fine with me to just allow it for unconstrained parameters.  We could also have log_center and log_scale for parameters constrained to be positive.  But in such settings it wouldn't kill the user to just define the parameter on the log scale.

I would, however, like to allow scales on vectors and matrices of unscaled parameters.  That could make sense.  Just for a simple example, imagine a model in which there are latent continuous test scores for each student.  We might want all these to be scaled with center=50 and scale=25, say.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] What to look for in pairs() diagnostic plots?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] What to look for in pairs() diagnostic plots?
messages.body_plain:
On Friday, February 24, 2017 at 9:03:41 PM UTC-5, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> It plots them in a separate color, I believe, but I'm
> clearly not up to date on the pairs plot any more.  One of
> the plots does this.  Then you can see if they're all in
> the neck of a funnel or on one side of a banana-shaped
> posterior, you can detect some problems.
>
> - Bob

Yeah divergences are plotted in red and hitting max-treedepth is indicated with yellow. There is also a new ggplot2-based version of the pairs plot that I pretty much have ready to go (https://github.com/stan-dev/bayesplot/pull/69). It will be released as part of the bayesplot package. The ggplot version will also give you more control over the appearance of the points indicating divergences and hitting max-treedepth (sometimes in the base R version they are hard to see).

On another note, the trace plots in the bayesplot package (the mcmc_trace function) allow you to add a rug plot that shows where the divergences occurred. This isn't always helpful, but it gives you a different way to look at the divergences that can complement what the pairs plot tells you. Here's a quick demonstration using rstanarm, but it works the same for models fit using rstan too:

library("rstanarm")

fit <- stan_glm(mpg ~ ., data = mtcars,
  # next line to keep example fast and also ensure we get some divergences
                prior = hs(), iter = 400, adapt_delta = 0.8)

# extract draws using as.array (instead of as.matrix) to keep
# chains separate for traceplot
posterior <- as.array(fit)

library("bayesplot")

# grab divergences ('nuts_params' is a convenience function in bayesplot)
divs <- nuts_params(fit, pars = "divergent__")
mcmc_trace(posterior, pars = "sigma", divergences = divs)

This results in the plots in the attached png file.

Jonah

messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] Variable Importance
messages.body_plain:
> On Feb 27, 2017, at 8:28 AM, smockin morry <smocki...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Stan Community,
> In predictive modelling often one encounters a large number of candidate predictors. But in order to achieve better predictive ability one would want to discard predictors that contributes very little in predicting a quantity of interest.

The main motivation I've seen for literally discarding predictors
is that they are collinear with other predictors or there's some
computation bound on which predictors you can use (if the data
has billions of predictors, as in subword data over large natural
language corpora, you need to prune those because 20GB predictor
vectors are impractical.

> A plot showing importance of variables helps in determining variables to be dropped from  a model. Have a look at the example in the following link https://topepo.github.io/caret/variable-importance.html. I am using MTCARS dataset in R as an example to try and achieve a plot such as the one below. Am wondering if there is a possibility of extracting ranks of predictors from Stan fit that can be plotted to produce such a plot as one below.

I'd suggest avoiding those ad-hoc selection metrics and reading Aki's
papers.  You know it's a bad idea when you see that it's an independent
evaluation.  You want to at least select variables stepwise, because what
you want is something that selects the "best" subset of variables.  It is
intractable done combinatorially, so people tend to do things like
rank reduction on the predictor matrices or impose L1 priors in the model
itself (or penalty function if you're an MLE sitckler).  Those convert the
discrete selection problem into something continuous where there's a hope
of solution.

You can see that one-at-a-time is bad by taking two collinear predictors
that are also collinear with the outcome.  The relative contribution of
x[2] after x[1] is quite low, even though independently they look very
"important".

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] counting/plotting divergent transitions
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] counting/plotting divergent transitions
messages.body_plain:
If you also want plots then I recommend checking out our new bayesplot package, which has several available plotting functions that give you some information about divergences.

The mcmc_nuts_divergence function compares the shape of lp__  (log-posterior up to constant) when there's a divergence (if there are any) to the distribution when there is no divergence. If there are divergences then you'll likely see that lp|divergence=1 will have much lighter tails than lp|divergence=0.

The mcmc_trace function now also accepts an optional argument divergences. If specified it will add a rug plot below the trace plot indicating the approximate location of the divergences.

Finally, the mcmc_pairs function (not yet released but available to try out <https://github.com/stan-dev/bayesplot/pull/69>) will indicate divergences as red points.

Jonah

Glad to see you got it running.

> I want to have 10 iterations but it just save 5 iterations. where's my mistake?

It's an unfortunate choice of output messages.

By default, Stan splits the iterations in half and does warmup for the
first half.  By default, it looks like StataStan's not saving the warmup
iterations.  So you only see the 5 sampling iterations.  The misleading thing
is that it says zero warmup iterations, when there are actually 5 warmup
iterations---the just don't get saved to file, so they're not visible to
the posterior analysis package here.

> N = length(ux);
> MCMC_dat = struct('N',N);
> initial = struct('x',ux');
> fit = stan('file','MC.stan','data',MCMC_dat,'chains',1,'iter',10,'init',initial,'algorithm','NUTS','sample_file','output-6.csv');

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

I was wondering if the automatic unconstraining transformations take amplification of rounding errors into account or if I don't need to worry about this.

So the problem I see is that whenever I declare a parameter to be positive, it is actually being sampled on the log space as far as I am aware. In my Stan program I get the exponential of it. Now, the gradients are being calculated wrt to the positive value and via the chain rule things are put back together. What worries me is that some functions which I use with the positive numbers are potentially not numerically very exact (e.g. ODEs is a classic example). Can this lead to an uncontrolled amplification of the rounding errors which makes the gradients in-exact?

In short: Is it beneficial to calculate straight on the unconstrained space whenever numerically less accurate functions are involved? So instead of modeling with (positive) rate constants, I should really work only with the logs of these and don't rely on automatic constraining and unconstraining. The price to pay then is that I have tons of exp expression in my code...

Anyone having some experience with this?

Thanks much.

Sebastian

Good afternoon!
I`m new Stan user. My question can be silly but I really need your help.

I`m writing a choice model with the following data in R: each individual offered С cards. Each card has K alternatives. So, each person need to choose 1 of the K alternatives on each card.

model_bayesian_multi_logit <- "
data {
    int N; // number of people
    int<lower=2> K; // number of alternatives on each card
    int<lower=1> D; // number of attributes that characterizes alternatives
    int<lower=1> C; // number of cards
    matrix[K, D] X[N, C]; // matriсes for different people and cards with all characteristics
    int y[N, C]; // each individual choices for each card
parameters {
    vector[D] beta;
}
model {
    for (d in 1:D)
        beta[d] ~ normal(0, 5);
    for (n in 1:N)
        for (c in 1:C)
        y[n, c] ~ categorical_logit(X[n, c]*beta);
}
"

Then I`m trying to check the model with the simplest example:
N <- 1
C <- 1
D <- 3
K <- 2
y <- 1
dim(y) <- c(1, 1)

X <- array(data = c(1, 1, 1.5, 1.5, 170, 250, 120, 150), dim = c(2, 3, 1, 1))
Where X looks like that (intuitively this is correct for the given N, C, D, K, because we got an array for only 1 person and 1 card, hence, 1 matrix in total)
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1  1.5  170

Individual is supposed to choose between 2 rows which characterizes 2 different alternatives.

fit_logit <- stan(model_code = model_bayesian_multi_logit, data = random_data, iter = 1000, chains = 4)

Stan tells me I`m wrong with X dimension:

Error in eval(substitute(expr), envir, enclos) :
  mismatch in dimension declared and found in context; processing stage=data initialization; variable name=X; position=0; dims declared=(1,1,2,3); dims found=(2,3,1,1)

I can rewrite X like that:
X <- array(data = c(1, 1, 1.5, 1.5, 170, 250, 120, 150), dim = c(1,1,2,3))

In this case Stan will work and give me the results but I think this is a wrong way (for the given example the answer looks right but for 1 person with 2 cards or more complicated cases it is wrong).

Well, I guess R and Stan have different perceptions of the dimension. Moreover, it seems that Stan stores arrays in a row-major order, while R in a column-major order.

> on the scale of the covariance matrix?  It does seem
> odd to just add this small number.

There are different recommendations. In case of MCMC and non-Gaussian likelihoods Radford Neal recommends quite a lot. In some specific cases and carefully implemented numerically stable computations, it's possible to manage with zero jitter. In some cases a good justification based on the floating point accuracy etc. is to have jitter slightly larger than sqrt(eps). Depending on these case I've used something between 1e-4 and 1e-8 (usually smaller).

Aki

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] When does the data dominates the posterior distribution?
messages.subject_clean: [stan-users] When does the data dominates the posterior distribution?
messages.body_plain:
This is good to think about for understanding, but in practice, isn't very useful.  We just want to put in a prior based on what we know.  It's just as much a part of the model as the likelihood, and we don't want to be thinking in terms of how we code it so it gets washed out.

You might be able to get a decent feel for what's going on with a simple conjugate example (let's say normal with fixed variance or a beta distribution).  You can see that where the prior starts and how much it's concentrated matters.  Michael Betancourt's about to roll out a nice case study where you can see how much the fatness of the prior's tails (Cauchy vs. normal, say) and the consistency of the prior (is the posterior concentrating in the trunk or the tails) make a big difference.

No idea about FNN.  KL-divergence requires computing an integral, which you
can compute in one direction with MCMC if you have draws from the posterior and
an analytic prior.   But you're probably better served by plotting out the
priors and posteriors and seeing how the latter concentrate as a function of
the prior and amount of data (and the variance in the data itself).

- Bob
